en: The Sūtra of the True Dharma of the Great Assembly Spoken by the Buddha,
Scroll One. Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Imperially Appointed Grand Officer of the Court of State Ceremonial, Acting Director of the Court of State Guests,
and Great Master of the Transmission of the Dharma, Subject Shi Hu, by Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of twelve thousand bhikṣus. These included the Venerable Ajñātakauṇḍinya, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Venerable Śāriputra, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, the Venerable Citta, the Venerable Rāhula, the Venerable Bhadrika, the Venerable Bhadrapāla, the Venerable Bhadraśrī, the Venerable Candraprabha, the Venerable Mahāsthāmaprāpta, the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, the Venerable Subhūti, the Venerable Revata, and the Venerable Candana; all of these were great arhats.
At that time, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, namely:

the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Maitreya, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Samantavīra, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Kumāraśrī, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Kumārasthita, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Kumārabhadra, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Anūnatva, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Samantabhadra, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Subhūti, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Vajrasena, and the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja; such was the assembly of sixty-two thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

Furthermore, there were twelve thousand hosts of devaputras, including the devaputra King of the Most Excellent Trees, the devaputra Virtuous, the devaputra Good Virtuous, the devaputra Love of Dharma, the devaputra Sandalwood Treasury, the devaputra Abiding in Fragrance, and the devaputra Sandalwood Incense, and others such as these.

Furthermore, there were eight thousand celestial maidens, including the celestial maiden Subhagā, the celestial maiden Atiśraddhā, the celestial maiden Īśvarī, the celestial maiden Śrīnetrā, the celestial maiden Lokasundarī, the celestial maiden Mahālokeśvarī, the celestial maiden Mahābalā, and the celestial maiden Subhujā, along with such a host of celestial maidens.

Furthermore, there were the Naga King Utpala, the Naga King Elapatra, the Naga King Timigila, the Naga King Vajra-śastra, the Naga King Uttama-śastra, the Naga King Priyaṃkara, the Naga King Succhada, and the Naga King Gajaśīrṣa; these and others, a multitude of eight thousand Naga Kings, all came together for this assembly.

Having arrived at the place where the Buddha was, they all bowed their heads to the ground to pay homage at the World-Honored One’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to sit on one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One remained silent.

At that time, there was in the assembly a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Puyong (Universal Valor), who rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, devas, humans, and other assemblies in this gathering have all assembled here, desiring to hear the Buddha proclaim the sublime Dharma.

This great multitude gazes with single-minded attention upon the exquisite physical marks of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, and delights in entering the Buddha-Dharma. Because they contemplate the Buddha’s marks with a mind that delights in the Dharma, those who have practiced for a long time are able to distance themselves from all obstructive defilements, while those who have newly begun their practice give rise to the resolve to cultivate supreme wholesome dharmas, never again momentarily conceiving unwholesome thoughts.
Having made this announcement, the Buddha then addressed the Bodhisattva Samantavīrya, saying:

"I possess a True Dharma named the Mahāsaṃnipāta, which shall be widely disseminated throughout Jambudvīpa. If there are sentient beings who hear it even for a moment, any of their grave offenses of the five heinous crimes shall be completely extinguished, and they shall no longer regress from Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Samantavīra! What do you think?
Do you consider that the mass of merit obtained by those who hear this Dharma is equal to that of a single Buddha?"
The Bodhisattva Samantavīra addressed the Buddha, saying: “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said, "Universal Valor!
Do not hold such a view; one who holds such a view does not have the true vision."
The Bodhisattva Samantavīra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how should one view it so that one may know that this person possesses a true accumulation of merit?”
The Buddha said, “Puyong!

The mass of merit obtained by those who hear this Dharma is equal, without any difference, to the mass of merit possessed by as many Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.”
Furthermore, Samantavīra!

Should there be anyone who hears this True Dharma, they shall all abide on the stage of non-retrogression; they will immediately be constantly observed by all Tathāgatas, and all Tathāgatas will always appear before them. Having subdued the armies of Māra and perfected the wholesome dharmas, such a person will be able to fully comprehend the principle of arising and ceasing, and all shall achieve Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the assembly of bodhisattvas rose from their seats and addressed the Buddha together, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is the measure of the mass of merit of a single Buddha?”
The Buddha said: "O sons of noble family!
Listen attentively."

Suppose there were a person who emptied the waters of the great ocean and sprinkled them all over Jambudvīpa; from these waters, they took a single drop and made it equal in number to the sands of a Ganges River. Continuing in this manner—one drop after another—until the entire water of the great ocean had been exhausted, each individual drop became a Ganges River. If every single one of these rivers were filled with as many grains of sand as there are in them, and every one of those grains of sand were a Bodhisattva dwelling on the tenth stage, would the mass of merit possessed by all those Bodhisattvas be great?
The assembly of bodhisattvas addressed the Buddha together, saying:
“It is very much so,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said, “O sons of good family!
The mass of merit of a single Buddha is even greater than that; and for those who hear the Dharma, it is multiplied many times over this number.”
Furthermore, sons of good family!

If there are sentient beings in the future final age who, upon hearing this true Dharma, give rise to a mind of faith and understanding, the mass of merit they obtain will be even greater than that, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Samantavīra rose again from his seat and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
For those sentient beings who delight in seeking the Dharma, how should they seek it?"
The Buddha said:
"Puyong! Those who seek the Dharma are, in brief, of two kinds:
"First, one gives rise to a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings; second, one explains the Dharma as it has been heard for the sake of sentient beings.
Bodhisattva Samantavīra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Furthermore, how should one explain the Dharma as it has been heard to sentient beings?
The Buddha said,
"Universal Valor!
There are also two kinds:
first, dedicating the Dharma one has heard toward enlightenment;
second, having a loving interest in seeking the Mahāyāna Dharma and persevering in it for a long time without the mind ever becoming weary or regressing.
"If one can thus preach for the sake of sentient beings, such a person is called a true seeker of the Dharma.
At that time, the assembly of devaputras and devakanyās within the gathering rose from their seats, stood before the Buddha, joined their palms toward him, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

With our profound resolve, we joyfully seek the True Dharma; just as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses great kindness and great compassion and is able to fulfill the heart's wishes of all sentient beings, we pray that you will extensively analyze and explain it for us.
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately emitted a great, rare, pure, and wondrous light within the assembly, universally illuminating the great multitude.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Samantavīra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
“For what cause and condition was this light emitted?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Samantavīra, saying:

“You should now know that within this assembly there are those who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, who perceive the Buddha, the World-Honored One, as one rarely encountered, and who, out of reverence and respect, entreat him to preach the Dharma. It is because of these causes and conditions that this light has been emitted.”
The Bodhisattva Samantavīra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
As for those sentient beings who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, how should they practice so as to achieve success?"
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent!

You are truly courageous that you are able to ask the Buddha, the World-Honored One, about this meaning amidst this great assembly. This will benefit all beings and enable them to swiftly attain the path of Buddhahood; through these roots of goodness, you too shall now achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Regarding what you have asked, I shall now explain it to you; you should listen attentively.

I recall that in the past, beyond incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), a Buddha appeared in the world named Ratnaśrī Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
At that time, I was a māṇavaka, establishing all sentient beings in the Buddha-wisdom.
Suddenly, on one occasion, I saw a deer king undergoing various sufferings and afflictions; at that moment, I secretly thought to myself:
"How might I be able to take these sufferings upon myself in place of this deer king?"
He further reflected:
"All sentient beings who revolve within the three realms and have not yet escaped suffering are likewise like this.
He then made this vow:

"May it be that when I have attained Buddhahood in the future, all sentient beings shall be free from all suffering and affliction, be born in my buddha-field, and dwell securely in the Buddha-wisdom.
Thus spoke Puyong!
"By the power of such roots of goodness and great vows, I have immediately attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, after the Bodhisattva Samantavīra had heard this teaching, he again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"At the time of that Buddha's world, what was the lifespan of sentient beings?
The Buddha said,
"The lifespan of sentient beings was a full eighty kalpas."
The Bodhisattva Samantavīra asked again:
"By what measure of kalpas does one attain that lifespan?
The Buddha said to Samantavīra:
"As for that measure of an eon (*kalpa*), it is, for example, like someone constructing a great city twelve *yojanas* wide and three *yojanas* high, and filling that city entirely with sesame seeds."

Suppose a person were to come once every hundred years, take a single sesame seed, and cast it outside; if they continued coming and casting seeds in this manner until all the sesame seeds were exhausted and even the city itself had been destroyed, the duration of this kalpa would still not have ended.

Furthermore, suppose there were a great mountain twenty-five *yojanas* wide and twelve *yojanas* high. A long-lived deva comes once every hundred years and sits upon it, brushing away the mountain stones with a *kauśika* garment. If he were to come and brush once in this manner until that mountain was entirely worn away, the measure of that eon would still not have reached its end.
“Samantavīra!
This is what is called the measure of a kalpa.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Samantavīra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If a person dedicates a single root of goodness toward bodhi and thereby obtains a great mass of merit, attaining a lifespan of eighty kalpas, how much more so for one who extensively practices within the Buddha’s profound and wondrous Dharma? The merit such a person obtains is beyond measure.”
The Buddha said to Pu Yong:

"If there are sentient beings who hear this True Dharma of the Great Assembly, they will obtain a lifespan of eighty-four thousand kalpas; how much more so for those who can further transcribe, read, and recite this True Dharma? The mass of merit they obtain will be many times greater than before, beyond all comparison."
Furthermore, Samantavīra!

If a person hears this True Dharma and gives rise to pure faith, reverence, and respect, that person will attain the knowledge of past lives for ninety-five kalpas and serve as a wheel-turning monarch for sixty thousand kalpas. They will be honored by all people and loved and respected by all; they cannot be harmed by blades, staves, poisons, or drugs. At the time of their death, the faces of ninety-five koṭis of Buddhas will appear before them to comfort that person, saying:
"Do not give way to fear; you have previously heard the True Dharma of the Great Assembly and possess a great mass of merit."

At that time, those ninety-five koṭis of Buddhas all bestowed upon him the prediction that each would be reborn within my buddha-field; how much more so for one who, by means of this True Dharma, causes it to be widely disseminated throughout the entire realm of sentient beings so that all may hear it.
The Bodhisattva Samantavīra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I now desire to hear and receive this True Dharma of the Great Assembly, my mind never wearying of it.”
The Buddha said, “Excellent, excellent!

Not only is your mind never weary of delighting in the Dharma, but I too am never weary of joyfully proclaiming this Dharma; how much less could any ordinary person ever conceive a sense of satiety regarding this True Dharma?”

Furthermore, Universal Valor! If there are sons or daughters of good family who give rise to deep faith and joy in this True Dharma, such persons shall not lose their right faith for a thousand kalpas; they shall not fall into the evil realms for five thousand kalpas; they shall remain far removed from delusion for twelve thousand kalpas; they shall not be born in border regions for eight thousand kalpas; they shall practice courageous giving for twenty thousand kalpas; they shall constantly be reborn in the celestial realms for twenty-five thousand kalpas; they shall constantly practice the Brahma-faring (celibacy) for twenty-five thousand kalpas; for forty thousand kalpas they shall remain far removed from the delusive bonds of kinship and shall not be obscured or clouded by afflictions; for fifty thousand kalpas they shall uphold the True Dharma; and for sixty-five thousand kalpas they shall abide securely in right mindfulness.
"Universal Valor!

Those sons and daughters of good family shall no longer give rise to the mind that commits sinful karma; no demons or adversaries shall be able to harm them, and wherever they are born, they shall not dwell within a womb."

Furthermore, if there are people who hear, receive, read, and recite this True Dharma, those people will attain full mastery of hearing and retention for eighty thousand kalpas; they will remain free from the karma of killing for one thousand kalpas, free from the karma of false speech for ninety-nine thousand kalpas, and free from the karma of divisive speech for thirteen thousand kalpas.
"Universal Valor, you should know that for this reason, this great and sublime Dharma is difficult to encounter; even its name is difficult to hear.

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Universal Valor, with even greater reverence, knelt with his right knee on the ground, prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“If there is someone who gives rise to contempt or slander toward this True Dharma, how much demerit will that person incur?
The Buddha said,
“It is exceedingly great.”
The Bodhisattva Samantavīra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How great is the number of offenses incurred by that person?
The Buddha said:

“Samantavīra! If a person were to give rise to a great evil mind toward Buddhas as numerous as the sands of twelve Ganges Rivers, their transgression would still be relatively light; however, if one gives rise to a mind of slight disparagement toward this True Dharma, the transgression incurred will be far greater than that.”
Why is this? Universal Valor!
If a person gives rise to contempt or slander toward that True Dharma, they are thereby initiating the mind that destroys the Mahāyāna and will burn themselves with the fire of afflictions.
The Bodhisattva Samantavīra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
All sentient beings are entangled by the habitual tendencies of their karma; they revolve through birth and death and are unable to attain liberation.”
The Buddha said to Universal Valor:
“It is so, it is so! It is like a person who cuts off their own head.”

At that time, there was a man who brought excellent medicines—namely, the excellent medicine *moci-ka*, the excellent medicine *yuni-nāva*, the excellent medicine *kṛtāva*, and the excellent medicine *dāri-nāva*—and applied such excellent medicines to the severed head.
"Samantavīra! What do you think?
Do you believe that this person's life will be restored?"
The Bodhisattva Samantavīra addressed the Buddha, saying: “No,
World-Honored One.”
"Even if such a person were to apply excellent medicine, how could they possibly survive? Universal Valor!
Those who revolve in saṃsāra are just like this."
"Furthermore, Universal Valor!

It is as if, at one time, there were two men, each holding a sharp blade, desiring to take the other's life; because they opposed one another with equal strength, neither was able to kill the other, yet they both suffered from wounds and extreme pain.
At that time, someone suddenly appeared carrying excellent medicine and applied it to their wounds; the sores were immediately healed.
Once the two men had recovered, they recalled their former suffering and said to one another:
"From this day forward, we shall never again give rise to the intent to kill or harm each other."

"O Samantavīra! All those who possess wisdom are likewise in this regard: although they may have committed karmic actions, they are immediately able to repent and do not turn their backs on the True Dharma; in this way, they gradually become able to advance toward all dharmas that transcend birth and death."
"Furthermore, Universal Courage!
Just as when people in the world have relinquished their life-span and karmic retribution, although their parents may grieve, lament, and weep, they can no longer serve as a refuge or a protector."

Those who are of the class of ordinary worldlings cannot benefit themselves, nor do they benefit others; their failure to cultivate wholesome karma is likewise so. At the time of death, they have no one to rely upon, and this is briefly of two kinds:
first, having personally committed various unwholesome karmas and further encouraging others to do so;
second, giving rise to a mind of contempt and slander toward the Buddha’s True Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Samantavīra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If there are those who give rise to a mind of contempt or slander toward the Buddha’s true Dharma, where will such persons fall when their lives end?”
The Buddha said to Samantavīra:

"Those who slander the Dharma, after their lives have ended, shall fall into the hells and undergo great suffering and affliction. That is to say, they shall suffer for one kalpa in each of the eight great hells: the Greatly Terrifying Hell, the Crushing Hell, the Heating Hell, the Intensely Heating Hell, the Black Rope Hell, the Avīci Hell, the Rumaharṣa Hell, and the Huhuva Hell."
The Bodhisattva Samantavīra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is most painful,
World-Honored One!”
"I cannot bear to hear this now.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for the Bodhisattva Samantavīra:
"The hells I have described, You find so terrifying you cannot bear to hear them."
Those sufferings of the hells are created by the karma of sentient beings themselves.
If one performs various wholesome deeds, one will certainly obtain the fruit of peace and happiness;
if one performs various unwholesome deeds, one will inevitably receive the retribution of suffering.
Bound by the suffering of birth and the suffering of death, And entangled by sorrows and grief,
Fools who fail to create the causes of happiness Are constantly afflicted by distress.
The wise attain peace and joy, For they have faith and delight in the Mahāyāna Dharma.
Reciting the Buddha’s name with supreme wisdom ensures one never falls into the evil realms.
Universal Courage, you should know that through the karmic conditions of past lives,
even by planting a single small root of virtue, one will certainly obtain a vast and great fruit.
Just as worldly seeds grow, And the hundred grains are never lost, So too,
when virtuous causes give rise to a Buddha-field, The fruits obtained are likewise so.
When the wise cultivate wholesome dharmas, They remain far removed from all causes of suffering.
He becomes the foundation of all virtues and attains the highest peace and happiness.
If one can practice impartial giving, even of the measure of a single hair’s breadth of wholesome Dharma,
for eighty thousand kalpas one will obtain vast wealth.
"In every place of rebirth, one should always mindfully practice giving;
because of giving to the Triple Gem, the retribution will unfold in succession without end.
At that time, having heard these verses spoken by the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Samantavīra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How may one come to understand and receive this True Dharma of the Great Assembly?
The Buddha said to Puyong:

“If a person has perfected roots of goodness in the presence of as many Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as there are grains of sand in twelve Gaṅgā rivers, they shall then be able to hear this sublime Dharma of the Great Assembly.”
The Bodhisattva Samantavīra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How can one attain such perfection of roots of goodness?”
The Buddha said to Samantavīra,
"If one can attain equal knowledge and vision regarding all Tathāgatas, this is the perfection of roots of goodness.
Samantavīra spoke again:
"How can one attain equal knowledge and vision regarding all Tathāgatas?
The Buddha said:
"If one respects and reveres the Dharma Master, one will thereby attain equal knowledge and vision regarding all Tathāgatas."
Samantavīra spoke again:
“Furthermore, how does one show respect and reverence toward the Dharma teacher?
The Buddha said:
"If a person gives rise to a mind directed toward the supramundane path, they shall respect and honor the Dharma teacher.
Universal Valor!
In such ways as these, one is able to bring all roots of goodness to fulfillment."
The Buddha said to Universal Valor:

“This True Dharma of the Great Assembly possesses great merit and benefits all beings. If there are those who can hear, receive, transcribe, read, or recite it, such persons shall obtain an immeasurable mass of great merit.”
"Universal Valor!

Even if there were as many Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas as there are grains of sand in twelve Ganges Rivers in each of the four directions, and they all remained for twelve kalpas preaching this sublime Dharma of the Great Assembly, one could never exhaustively describe the merit of hearing and receiving it."

Furthermore, in each of the four directions, there are likewise Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River; even if they were all to remain for the aforementioned eons expounding the merit of this transcription, they could not exhaust it.

Furthermore, in each of the four directions, there are Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, who all remain for the aforementioned eons and expound this merit of recitation, yet they do not reach its end.
The Bodhisattva Samantavīra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We pray that the Buddha will briefly explain the mass of merit from reciting [this sutra]; how great is its number?”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"If a person can read and recite even a single four-line verse,
the mass of merit they obtain shall equal that of those eighty-four [thousand]."
The mass of merit of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges is equal and without distinction;
how much more so for one who can dwell with a single mind in the True Dharma—
their mass of merit shall be inexhaustible.
"Buddhas appear in the world and proclaim boundless teachings, yet it is truly difficult to encounter them.
At that time, eighteen koṭis of Nirgrantha followers came to where the Buddha was, all entered the assembly, and each sat to one side, saying: "Gautama!
"We are superior to you!
Thus they spoke three times, each time saying:
"We are superior to you!"
At that time, the Buddha addressed the assembly of Nirgranthas, saying:
"Only the Buddha, the Tathāgata, has attained the name of 'True Victor,' for there is no one who can surpass him in any respect."
The Nirgrantha said, "How can you alone, Gautama, be victorious?
The Buddha said:
“If you, Nigaṇṭhas, are certain that you have attained victory, this is a perverted view and not a true view.
By what means do you consider yourselves victorious? Speak freely.”
At that time, the assembly of Nirgranthas were all silent, looking at one another in secret.
The Buddha said:

"You should know that only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, among all sentient beings—whether they have already entered the Buddha’s wisdom or have not yet entered it, whether their faculties are sharp or dull—enables them all to attain liberation. He benefits them with equality, without distinction; this is what can be called 'the Invincible One.'"
Reflect well: when you are oppressed by the various sufferings within your own body and mind, you are not even aware of them; how then can you claim superiority?
I shall now show you the subtle, vast, and sublime True Dharma of all Buddhas.
When the various Nigaṇṭhas heard these words of the Buddha, they were suddenly seized with great anger and gave rise to a lack of faith.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, while residing in the Sudharmā Hall, saw this with his divine eye; he immediately took up his vajra and entered the assembly, intending to destroy it.
All the Nigaṇṭhas were filled with alarm and fear; they were overcome with great distress and wept for a long time.

At that moment, the World-Honored One vanished from the midst of the great assembly. Just as the Nigaṇṭhas had begun to look up toward the Buddha, the World-Honored One suddenly disappeared from their sight. Their sorrow and suffering increased all the more, and they spoke these verses:
"Just like a person dwelling alone In a desolate and empty wilderness..."
Without father and without mother, one fears there is no one to provide rescue.
Like a great river devoid of water, where the swimming fish have nowhere to rely;
like all trees broken and shattered, where the flying birds have nowhere to rest.
"We are now filled with fear, and our suffering is likewise;
not seeing the Buddha, the World-Honored One, who will be our protector?

At that time, after the assembly of Nirgranthas had spoken these verses, they wished to rise from their seats. Just as their two kneecaps touched the ground, the earth where they touched it suddenly let out a great sound, causing the entire assembly of humans and devas to tremble.
All the Nirgranthas thought to themselves:
"The Tathāgata, the most supreme among two-legged beings, we pray that out of compassion you will rescue and deliver us.
At that moment, the World-Honored One immediately manifested his body and returned to his original seat, and addressed the Bodhisattva Samantavīra, saying:
“You should preach the Dharma to the assembly of Nirgranthas and transform them.
The Bodhisattva Samantavīra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“No, World-Honored One.”
World-Honored One!
For example, the King of Mountains, Sumeru, is supremely wonderful, lofty, and prominent; yet there are small black mountains situated at its side—how could one say they are equal to it?
"Now, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, dwells amidst the great assembly; his dispatching me to preach the Dharma is likewise so.
The Buddha said, "Stop!"
"Stop! Good son! The skillful means of the Tathāgata, whatever he has taught throughout the worlds of the ten directions, is all established by the power of the Tathāgata’s compassion and vows."
"These Nirgranthas and others take delight in me; I shall preach the essential Dharma of the Unsurpassed for them. Samantavīra!
You should now go to the worlds of the ten directions, draw near to the Buddhas, and proclaim the transformative teachings of the Dharma."
The Bodhisattva Samantavīra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
My supernatural powers are exceedingly meager; were it not for the Buddha’s great compassion lending me his divine power, I would ultimately be unable to proceed.”
The Buddha said to Samantavīra, “Now,
by means of your own supernormal powers and the Buddha’s spiritual power, you may go in this manner. Receiving the Buddha’s holy command,
the Bodhisattva Samantavīra rose from his seat, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and suddenly vanished from the assembly, his body no longer visible.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the assembly of Nirgranthas, saying:
"You should know this: birth is a great suffering. Because of the suffering of birth, various fears arise; namely, because of birth there is the fear of illness;
because of the fear of illness, there is the fear of old age."
Because there is the fear of old age, there is the fear of death.
For what reason is birth feared?
It is because one is oppressed by manifold sufferings.
With birth as the cause, there arise all manner of fears.
If the phenomenon of birth did not exist, from what would fear arise?

Consequently, there are the fears of royal calamities, the fears of banditry, the fears of poisons, the fears of fire, the fears of water, the fears of wind, and even the fears of thunder and hail; furthermore, there are the fears arising from one's own unwholesome karmic actions.
"Such fears as these arise because of birth; if one thoroughly understands the nature of birth, one immediately becomes free from all fears.

At that time, after the World-Honored One had briefly explained this Dharma of fear to the assembly of Nirgranthas, the assembly of Nirgranthas was suddenly awakened to understanding. They repented their errors and reproached themselves, and together they addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We were ignorant and gave rise to improper views; turning our backs on the true path and contravening the Buddha’s True Dharma, we have committed a profound transgression. We pray that the Buddha, out of his great compassion, will accept us.”

Having spoken these words, the eighteen koṭis of Nirgrantha followers simultaneously gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Immediately, they all became a multitude of eighteen koṭis of great Bodhisattvas, each attaining the perfection of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Then, by means of their supernormal powers (*ṛddhibala*), they each manifested various miraculous transformations and various bodies:

the body of a Buddha, the body of a Bodhisattva, the body of a Pratyekabuddha, and the body of a Śrāvaka; even the bodies of devas, humans, nāgas, spirits, and all other classes of beings. Having done so, they each transformed themselves into precious lotus thrones, sharing half of them on either side of the Buddha. After prostrating at the Buddha’s feet, they each sat upon their respective seats.
The Sūtra on the True Dharma of the Great Assembly Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll One.
The Sūtra on the True Dharma of the Great Assembly Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Two.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Imperial Court Attendant, Acting Director of the Court of State Ceremonial.
Translated by the Imperial Preceptor for Transmitting the Dharma, the Subject Shi Hu, by imperial decree:

At that time, after the World-Honored One had converted the assembly of Nirgranthas, he employed skillful means and eloquent dharma-teachings, abiding in *samāhita* concentration, extending his golden-hued arm for seven days and nights. This continued until the Bodhisattva Samantavīra, having traveled through the worlds of the ten directions and extensively performed Buddha-deeds, returned to this land.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Samantavīra, from that Lotus-Flower Supreme Buddha-field, arrived before the Buddha in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm; having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and circumambulated him three times to the right, he stood to one side.
At that time, when the World-Honored One had emerged from samādhi, the Bodhisattva Samantavīra came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Having received the Buddha’s command, I traveled to those worlds of the ten directions; by my own supernatural power, I passed through ninety-nine thousand koṭis of buddha-fields, and by the Buddha’s supernatural power, I further passed through a hundred thousand koṭis of buddha-fields, until finally arriving at the world Padmottara in the nadir.”
Passing through eight thousand koṭis of Buddha-fields, he beheld those Buddhas manifesting great supernatural powers;
further passing through ninety-two thousand koṭis of Buddha-fields, he saw the Tathāgatas manifesting for the sake of sentient beings by preaching the profound and wondrous Dharma.

Furthermore, having passed beyond eighty thousand koṭis of buddha-fields, at one time I beheld eighty thousand koṭis of Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas appearing in the world; at that time, I paid respectful homage and made offerings before each and every one of those Buddhas.

Furthermore, having passed beyond thirty-nine koṭis of Buddha-fields, I beheld thirty-nine thousand koṭis of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas appearing simultaneously, all of whom had realized *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Toward each of those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who had first attained the Way, I paid homage, prostrated, and made offerings with reverence; thereafter, by means of my own supernatural power, I concealed my body so that it was no longer visible.
Furthermore, having passed beyond sixty koṭis of Buddha-fields, I beheld each of those Tathāgatas and paid them my respects one by one.
Again, having passed beyond a hundred koṭis of Buddha-fields, I saw those Buddhas entering parinirvāṇa; at that time, I once more paid homage and made offerings to each of them individually.
From here, passing through ninety-five more Buddha-fields, I learned that those Tathāgatas had all long since entered parinirvāṇa and that their true Dharma was on the verge of being destroyed.
At that time, I reflected to myself in secret:
"That the true Dharma of these Buddhas is about to perish is a profound and great suffering."
Having formed this thought, he gave rise to great compassion.
At that time, there were also devas, humans, nāgas, spirits, yakṣas, and others from the desire and form realms who all felt profound distress.

Furthermore, he saw therein one buddha-field where the True Dharma of that Buddha had long since been extinguished. The kalpa-fire blazed forth from all four sides; even the great earth, Sumeru the king of mountains, the great oceans, the rivers, and all trees were completely incinerated. With nothing left to rely upon, there remained only the empty realm, vast and boundless.

"Having passed beyond these lands, one arrives at the lower direction; in a single world, one sees hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Tathāgatas, each seated upon a precious lotus throne. Furthermore, seeing the four directions in the same manner, those various Buddhas each manifest to teach the Dharma and deliver all sentient beings."
“World-Honored One!
Once I had arrived at that buddha-field, I immediately thought:
‘What is the name of this buddha-field now?’”
There was a certain Buddha who addressed me, saying:
"Good son! This present buddha-field is named Lotus Superior."
I then asked: "World-Honored One who manifested this transformation, what is your name?
That Buddha replied:
"He is named Padmagarbha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
At that time, I prostrated to them all with single-minded reverence and addressed them thus:

"I now behold these hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Buddhas, each seated upon a precious lotus throne; yet I do not know which one among them is the Buddha named Padmagarbha. I only pray that you will show me the World-Honored One who is my transformation-master."
At that time, the Tathāgata Padmagarbha spoke these words among the many Buddhas:
"Good son! The Buddha Padmagarbha is none other than my own self."
Having spoken these words, those Buddhas and others each suddenly concealed their Tathāgata bodies and manifested the forms of Bodhisattvas.

At that time, I saw only the emanation-master, the Tathāgata Padmagarbha; this one Buddha, the World-Honored One, sat amidst the great assembly, his marks and signs and majestic spiritual power such that none could surpass him.
I immediately prostrated myself with my head at his feet in reverent salutation.
At that time, that Buddha pointed to the lotus seat and said to me,
"O son of good family!
"You may take this seat.

"At that time, having taken my seat, I immediately saw that Buddha, and on his left and right there were immeasurable precious lotus seats, exquisitely adorned and most rare. Suddenly, this thought occurred to me:
'How is it that these seats are all empty, with no one able to ascend them?'"
He then questioned that Buddha,
who replied to me, saying:
"O son of good family!

These seats are all established through inconceivable, supreme, and wondrous merits; they cannot be accomplished by those with meager roots of goodness. If there are persons who have not yet entered even a portion of the Buddha-dharma, they cannot even see them, let alone ascend upon them.
At that time, I again asked the World-Honored One:
"What roots of goodness should one plant to be able to ascend to such thrones?
That Buddha replied:

“Good son! If there are those who can even briefly listen to and receive this True Dharma of the Great Assembly, they shall ascend this seat by virtue of these roots of goodness; how much more so for those who can further copy it, recite it, and constantly practice it.”

"Good son! Throughout immeasurable kalpas in the past, you have already been able to receive and uphold such a True Dharma of the Great Assembly. Had it not been for the power of these roots of goodness, I would not yet have reached this buddha-field, much less seen this seat and desired to ascend upon it."
After that Buddha had spoken these words, I immediately said to him: "So it is, so it is!
World-Honored One."
I again asked that Buddha:
"How many merits does this True Dharma of the Great Assembly possess, such that it can give rise to all wholesome dharmas?
At that time, the Tathāgata Padmagarbha also emitted a rare, pure, and wondrous radiance that universally illuminated the assembly of Buddhas, and having done so, he spoke to me, saying:

“Good son! You, a great Bodhisattva, have attained great power and unimpeded wisdom; you are able to proclaim the Buddha’s deeds for the sake of all sentient beings throughout all Buddha-lands. Previously, you already questioned Śākyamuni Tathāgata of this Sahā world regarding this Dharma, and now you ask me about it once again. I shall explain it to you in detail as well. For example, suppose there were a person who placed sesame seeds throughout the four great continents until they were completely filled, and these were then combined into a single heap—would this not be a great amount?”
I immediately replied: "Very many,
World-Honored One!"
Then that Buddha said:
"Suppose there were a person who took a single sesame seed and placed it in another location, and in this manner, taking one after another, wished to know their total number."
"Good son! What do you think?
Would such a person be able to know their number?"
I replied again: "No, World-Honored One!"
"Even if this person were to exhaust all their strength for many kalpas, they would ultimately be unable to know such a quantity.
That Buddha spoke again: "Good son!..."

The mass of merit of this True Dharma of the Great Assembly is likewise beyond what can be known through calculation or analogy. Even if as many Buddhas, Tathāgatas, as described above were each to spend koṭis of nayutas of kalpas weighing and praising the merits of hearing and receiving this Great True Dharma, they could not exhaust them; how much more so for one who writes it down, reads it, or recites it—their merit is exceedingly vast.
I asked again: "If one were to transcribe it, how much merit would they obtain?
I pray that the Buddha will briefly explain this."
At that time, that Buddha said:
"Good son! Suppose all the grasses, trees, and forests in a trichiliocosm were entirely cut into pieces the size of a single finger-joint, and each such piece were a universal monarch (cakravartin);"

Furthermore, suppose all the earth and stones in a trichiliocosm were ground into fine dust, and each particle of dust were a universal monarch (cakravartin). If mathematicians and the like were to wish to know the total number of such accumulations of merit, do you think such a person could know that number?
I then replied: "No, World-Honored One!"
“Even mathematicians and the like cannot calculate such a mass of merit.
That Buddha further said:

“If there is anyone who writes down this True Dharma of the Great Assembly, the mass of merit they obtain will likewise be such, and even more than that, beyond what can be known through calculation or analogy.”
If one can merely write down a single word of this True Dharma, the mass of merit obtained by that person already surpasses the former;

how much more so for anyone who receives and upholds even a single four-line verse of this True Dharma? The merit of such a person is beyond measure or calculation: all treasuries of jewels will constantly appear before them, all afflictions will be completely extinguished, the light of the torch of all dharmas will shine everywhere, no celestial Māras will be able to overcome them, and they will be able to enter all dharma-gates observed by all Bodhisattvas.
After that Buddha had spoken thus, I immediately said to him: "World-Honored One!

If there are sentient beings who are able to practice correctly within such a Great Assembly of the True Dharma, they may be called those who practice the supreme Brahma-conduct; and that Brahma-conduct is itself the conduct of the Tathāgata. If one diligently practices it without interruption, such a person will have a hundred Buddha-Tathāgatas constantly appearing before them day and night. Upon seeing the Tathāgatas, they immediately enter the Buddha-fields; having entered the Buddha-fields, they will be able to fully comprehend all treasuries of the Dharma."
"After I had spoken these words at that time, the Buddha Padmagarbha addressed me again, saying:

'Good son! The appearance of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, occurs but once in an age; even to encounter one is difficult. To preach this True Dharma is even more difficult, and to hear and uphold it is most difficult of all.'"
Why is this? If there are those who hear this true Dharma, for sixty thousand, six hundred, and eighty kalpas,
they will either attain the knowledge of past lives, or become a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin), Śakra, or a deity of the Pure Light Heaven (Śuddhāvāsa).
The Great Brahmā World-Lord and others are able to maintain unshakable right faith, avoid falling into the evil realms, and not be born as asuras.
They are free from strife with weapons or staves, and having distanced themselves from ignorance, they attain great wisdom.
Their marks and signs are upright and majestic, just like those of the Buddhas; each and every physical characteristic is identical and without difference.
They will not be entangled by the delusions and afflictions of kinsmen; they will always be free from the suffering of illness and constantly attain the divine eye.

They will not be reborn as *nāgas*, nor will they give rise to anger. Furthermore, they will always remain far removed from all poverty and destitution, enjoying great happiness as a copper-wheel-turning monarch (*tāmra-cakravartin*).
With their sense faculties perfected and endowed with patience, this shall continue until the time of their death.
At the time of death, right mindfulness will appear before them and their minds will not be inverted.

At that moment, Buddhas as numerous as the sands of twelve Gaṅgā rivers will manifest their faces before them from the east; twenty Gaṅgā-sands of Buddhas from the south; twenty-five Gaṅgā-sands of Buddhas from the west; eighty Gaṅgā-sands of Buddhas from the north; ninety thousand koṭis of Buddhas from above; and one hundred koṭis of Buddhas from below. All such Buddhas will appear before him to comfort that person, all saying these words: "O son of good family!..."

Do not give rise to fear; you have already possessed great merit as your refuge. Do you now see these hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Buddha-Bhagavāns, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges?
He replied, “I see them. Then the Buddhas said:
“Good son! It is by the power of your merit that all these Tathāgatas have come here together.
That person spoke again:
"By the power of what roots of goodness do I now obtain such [a result]?
Those Buddhas replied,
"It is by the power of the great roots of goodness from your long-standing hearing of the True Dharma of the Great Assembly."
That person further said:

"If even a single individual like me, by merely hearing the True Dharma, attains such immeasurable merit, how much more so for one who can cause the entire realm of sentient beings to hear and know it universally?"
"At that time, after the Tathāgata Padmagarbha had extensively described how that person at the point of death sees the various Buddhas, he further addressed me, saying:
'O son of good family!'"

If a person hears even a single four-line verse of this great, sublime Dharma, the mass of merit they obtain will be equal and no different from that acquired by making offerings to as many Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas as there are grains of sand in thirteen Gaṅgā rivers.

Furthermore, if there are those who hear this True Dharma of the Great Assembly, the mass of merit they acquire is as follows: suppose the entire trichiliocosm were filled to capacity with sesame seeds, and each of these sesame seeds were a universal monarch (cakravartin).

Suppose there were a person who bestowed various precious jewels as alms upon each of these wheel-turning kings; the mass of merit obtained from that would not equal that of giving to a single *srotāpanna*.
Giving to a single *srotāpanna* is not equal to giving to as many *srotāpannas* as previously described, filling the entire trichiliocosm;
and giving to such *srotāpannas* is not equal to giving to a single *sakṛdāgāmin*.
If one were to give to a single *sakṛdāgāmin*, it would not be as meritorious as giving to as many *sakṛdāgāmins* as previously described, filling the entire trichiliocosm;
if one were to give to such *sakṛdāgāmins*, it would not be as meritorious as giving to a single *anāgāmin*;
if one were to give to a single *anāgāmin*, it would not be as meritorious as giving to as many *anāgāmins* as previously described, filling the entire trichiliocosm.
If one were to give to such an Anāgāmin, it would not equal giving to a single Arhat;
if one were to give to a single Arhat, it would not equal giving to as many Arhats as previously described filling the entire trichiliocosm;
if one were to give to such Arhats, it would not equal giving to a single Pratyekabuddha.
If one were to give to a single pratyekabuddha, it would not be as meritorious as giving to all the pratyekabuddhas filling a trichiliocosm, in the same quantity as previously described;
if one were to give to such pratyekabuddhas, it would not be as meritorious as giving to a single bodhisattva;
and if one were to give to a single bodhisattva, it would not be as meritorious as giving to all the bodhisattvas filling a trichiliocosm, in the same quantity as previously described.
If one were to give alms to such bodhisattvas, it would not equal the merit of giving with pure faith and making offerings to a single Tathāgata;

if one makes offerings with faith to a single Tathāgata, it would not equal the merit of making offerings with faith to all the Tathāgatas as numerous as those previously mentioned who fill the trichiliocosm;

yet even though one makes offerings with faith to all these Tathāgatas, it would not equal the merit obtained by someone who briefly hears and retains this True Dharma of the Great Assembly, for the mass of merit gained is many times greater than that—how much more so if one can further copy, read, or recite it? Such merit is beyond measure.
At that time, that Buddha further addressed me, saying:
"Good son! You should conceive pure faith in this True Dharma and proclaim it far and wide."
Ordinary worldlings are unable to hear this True Dharma; even if some should hear it, they give rise to doubt and lack faith—how, then, could they enter this great mass of the Dharma?
"It is as if there were a person who entered the great ocean, desiring to see its very limits; do you think such a person would be able to see them? I replied, "No."
“World-Honored One!
Furthermore, suppose there were a person standing at the edge of the great ocean who, using his hand to scoop up water, wished to dry it up completely.
Do you think such a person could succeed?”
I replied again: "No, World-Honored One!"

These foolish people, though they wish to know the limits of the ocean and desire to exhaust it until it dries up, will ultimately fail; they merely exhaust themselves in vain and suffer a profound and great loss.
Then that Buddha said:

"All classes of ordinary beings are likewise thus; they are unable to hear and receive this True Dharma, and within the ocean of birth and death they falsely give rise to perversions and increase their ignorance. This is a profound and great loss."

Although hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas may appear in the world, such a person does not plant roots of goodness; they do not get to see the Buddhas, do not hear this Dharma, and are not protected and remembered by the Buddhas.

If there is a wise person who can give rise to pure faith in the presence of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Buddhas, and seeing those Buddhas feels great joy, and then hears this Dharma from those Buddhas; having heard this Dharma, they understand it as it truly is and do not give rise to disparagement or slander—such a person attains great and wholesome benefit, and is protected and remembered by all the Buddhas together.

If there is a person who, regarding this True Dharma, is able to hear, receive, or transcribe even a single four-line verse, that person shall, after passing beyond ninety-five thousand koṭis of Buddha-fields, be born in the World of Ultimate Bliss to behold the Buddha and hear the Dharma, with a lifespan of eighty-four thousand kalpas.
That Buddha Padmagarbha further addressed me, saying:

"If a person commits the five heinous crimes—whether acting upon them themselves, inciting others to do so, or seeing or hearing them and rejoicing in them—that person shall undergo the suffering of the five states of immediate retribution;
yet if there is one who hears even a single four-line verse of this True Dharma of the Great Assembly, such karma as these will be immediately extinguished."
At that time, that Buddha further proclaimed these verses for me:
"Listen now as I speak of the merit of hearing this sutra.
In a past kalpa, there was a person who committed all five kinds of karma."
That is to say: killing one's father, harming one's mother, breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha, destroying the bodhisattva’s samādhi, and corrupting the Tathāgata’s true wisdom.
If such a person commits these sins and subsequently gives rise to remorse, [they may still attain purification].
Afflicted with grief, he wept again and gave rise to this thought:
"I have committed manifold evil deeds; not only will this body be destroyed, but in future lives and for many eons, my bodies shall all be ruined."
From suffering arises suffering; the experience of suffering becomes ever deeper.
Having distanced oneself from virtuous friends, one is held in contempt by the world.
Both mundane and supramundane dharmas—I have utterly incinerated them all.
The roots of goodness cultivated over immeasurable eons, once destroyed, do not increase.
Like a worldly dwelling adorned with myriad colors that is suddenly consumed by fire, all people lose their love and delight for it.
It is the same for me when I commit a transgression; in this world and the next, I am consumed by the fires of karma, bringing neither joy nor delight to myself or others.
In every life I am born into, I am reviled, cursed, and beaten by men.
Constantly impoverished, hungry, and thirsty, they are assailed by a multitude of sufferings.
Such retributions as these are not induced by any other cause;
they all arise from the five karmas, for the fruits of unwholesome deeds never fail to manifest.
"Now that my suffering is thus, who is there to provide protection?
My friends and kin lack the power; I have no refuge whatsoever.
He then reflected further:
"I would rather go now to the summit of that high mountain and end this life by casting myself down,
so as to avoid increasing my evil karma and being reborn in suffering—
both in this world and in the next— ruined by my own misdeeds."
"Since there is no refuge within, it is likewise without one without;
manifesting now as the cause of transgression, one shall receive the most grievous retribution.
Having formed this thought, he wept once more.
Immediately, from within the void, a celestial being proclaimed: "Alas!
There is no refuge and no savior; you have yourself performed the five karmas."
Having killed your father and harmed your mother, you now undergo this suffering yourself;
why do you harbor such thoughts as wishing to end your life by leaping from a high mountain?
I now exhort you: do not give rise to such deluded views.
Simply give rise to a mind of repentance; why need you harm your own body and life?
Greed, hatred, and delusion—the three poisons—arise from your own mind;
the suffering and affliction within the evil realms cannot be avoided by any other means.
Though you may wish to sacrifice your life, it cannot be called true diligence;
in this state, your life will quickly end, and the retribution for evil will swiftly arise.
Listen now to my words, as I shall provide you with a skillful means.
The noble path of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, you have not yet been able to enter.
Now you should go to a mountain, a place where sages practice;
you should personally pay them homage, for they are able to provide protection.
There is a most excellent expedient, namely the sublime and correct Dharma,
which can cause one to leave behind all fears and eliminate the most evil karma.
At that time, having heard the voice from the sky, that person—
He immediately went to the mountains, to the place where the seer practiced his austerities.
Upon arrival, he saw a seer; he immediately prostrated himself with his head at the seer's feet, joined his palms, and spoke these words:
Terrified by suffering and affliction, I have committed the five most grave karmas;
I shall surely fall into the evil realms.
How may I escape and be free from them?
Throughout the day and night, whether eating, drinking, sitting, or lying down,
I have constantly been distressed by the suffering of existence,
finding not even a moment’s slight joy. Now, I have given rise to faith and reverence toward the Rishi.
"As I have asked, I pray that you, O Seer, will explain it to me:
Having committed many evil karmas, how can they be extinguished?
Then that Seer replied:
"I shall answer what you ask me.
At that time, the seer, having finished his meal and washed his hands and feet,
sat down cross-legged and listened as the other confessed of his own accord.
That person then circumambulated him to the right, paid homage to the Sage, and withdrew to sit down.
He declared: "I was foolish; I killed my father and harmed my mother.
I broke the harmony of the Saṃgha and destroyed the Bodhisattva’s samādhi."
Having destroyed the Tathāgata’s perfect wisdom, you have committed these five kinds of karma.
When the seer heard this speech, he spoke immediately:
"You are truly an unwholesome person, having committed such sins as these."
Hearing the words of the seer, that person again gave rise to anxiety and distress;
fearing there was no rescue, he thought he would surely fall into the evil realms.
At that moment, he rose from his seat and prostrated at the feet of the seer.
Once again, he gave rise to deep reverence and spoke these words:
"O Seer, have compassion for me, whose karma was exceedingly grave.
My doubts and afflictions are profound; I pray only that you will be my refuge."
"Though I have repented in this way, I lack the means for deliverance;
O Great Compassionate Sage, may my sins be extinguished.
Having heard these words, the Sage comforted that person, saying:
"Do not fear now; I am able to provide protection for you.
I shall guide you with single-minded devotion to cause you to leave all sufferings behind and to have your heavy transgressions extinguished. I am indeed your refuge."
"The Buddha possesses a wondrous Dharma gate called the Great Assembly;
it is the supreme skillful means—have you not heard of it before?
That person replied to the seer:
"I have never heard this before.
The seer spoke again: "Alas for those of sinful karma!
Like a person whose body has already been consumed by fire, who indeed would preach the Dharma for them?"
Now, with a heart of compassion, I shall show you the subtle and wondrous Dharma;
you should listen well.
I recall a time in the past, beyond immeasurable and boundless *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
At that time there was a king, named Vimalacandra;
his retinue was most flourishing, and he ruled the world with the True Dharma. Once, the king gave birth to a son.
He immediately ordered a physiognomist to be summoned to examine the child’s auspicious and inauspicious marks.
He then asked the physiognomist:
"Regarding this son of mine, as for his marks of goodness or evil, what do you observe?"
The physiognomist stepped forward and said:
"How strange is this child!
According to my observations, his marks are most inauspicious!"
The King spoke again: "What are these inauspicious signs?
Tell me truly and in detail according to the signs you have observed."
The physiognomist spoke thus:
"When this child reaches the age of seven, he will give rise to a mind of deluded malice and take the lives of his own parents."
The King spoke again:
"I would rather sacrifice my own body and life; this child shall never be harmed.
If I were to abandon him, I would no longer return to the human realm."
He immediately commanded his kinsmen, "Raise my son well.
Thereafter, that boy gradually grew up; at that time, Vimalacandra recalled the words of the physiognomist.
He immediately gave rise to this thought:
"Now my karma is likely to reach its fruition; what could I possibly begrudge!
Having formed this thought, he then commanded his son: "You shall now succeed me to the throne."
He spoke again to the youth:
"Now, this realm of mine is vast and exceedingly extraordinary;
like the sun and moon illuminating the world, it is wealthy, noble, and autonomous."
"Now this Tiṣya of mine, I entrust entirely to you;
within this realm, I shall no longer possess anything.
When the ministers and servants suddenly heard these words, they...
They came before Vimalacandra and all addressed him thus:
"O our Honored One, for what reason now have you abandoned your sphere of activity? What do you know to be the cause of this?"
"I pray that the Honored One will explain this to me. Vimalacandra replied:
"You should now know this: the entrusting of Upatiṣya to his son was likewise not without cause or condition."
I recall in the past, there was a king named Padma;
his realm was exceedingly vast, and he was sovereign and wealthy. At one time, he too begot a son.
As he gradually grew up, he immediately harmed his parents.
If I do not now give this Tiṣya to my son,
he shall suffer immeasurable anguish, just like that lotus.
I have constantly reflected upon this, and I should not give rise to regret;
for these reasons, I shall now entrust it to him.
At that time, that seer, who had performed the fivefold service, [received it].
Having explained these causes and conditions, he further addressed that person, saying:
"The five karmas you have now committed are far more grievous than those;
moved by a heart of compassion, I shall devise skillful means for you."
You should go to the Buddha’s presence and listen to the Dharma of the Great Assembly;
if you are able to hear and receive it, all karmic offenses will be extinguished.
All obstacles of affliction will be entirely rendered unimpeded.
By hearing the true Dharma, one avoids falling into the evil realms.
If a person can listen with a single-minded focus to even a single four-line verse of this Great Assembly Dharma, they shall obtain an immeasurable mass of merit.
The grave sins of the five heinous acts are extinguished, and one attains vast karmic rewards;
all veils and fetters are liberated in a single instant.
At that time, the person who had committed those deeds, having heard what the seer said, [was transformed].
Thereupon, with palms joined in reverence, he bowed his head to the ground with a single-minded devotion and uttered this praise: "Excellent!"
"O virtuous friend!
You have been able to guide and show me the Dharma-gate of the Great Assembly.
When the Rishi had finished speaking these words, there were then twelve thousand [who attained realization].
The assembly of devaputras came to the place of the rishi;
each paid homage with palms joined and bowed their heads at the rishi’s feet.
Furthermore, there were four koṭis of great nāga kings.
They also came to the place where the Seer was and prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet.
Furthermore, eighteen thousand koṭis of yakṣa kings came to the place where the Seer was and likewise prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet.
They all spoke these words together:
"You have profoundly realized all Buddha-dharmas and skillfully opened the gates to the celestial realms;
you have extinguished billions of kalpas of suffering in the three miserable paths."
I praise this Great Assembly, the subtle and supreme Dharma,
which possesses extraordinary merit and can extinguish all grave offenses.
If a person, regarding even a single verse, listens to it with sympathetic joy and accepts it, [they shall attain great benefit].
One may then be called a person who has deeply planted roots of goodness;
how much more so for one who, with single-minded devotion, gives rise to respect and reverence,
offering flower garlands, unguents, and powdered sandalwood incense.
With precious canopies, banners, and streamers, one makes offerings to this True Dharma;
whether acting for oneself or exhorting others, or seeing and hearing it and giving rise to sympathetic joy—
the various meritorious rewards obtained therein shall be vast and inexhaustible.
"Excellent, you seer, you who are truly endowed with compassion! Having offered this praise,
the assembly of devas and nāga kings, as well as the yakṣa kings and others,
paid homage to the seer and vanished from sight.

At that time, after the Bodhisattva Samantavīra had extensively expounded before Śākyamuni Buddha these merits of the True Dharma of the Great Assembly as praised by the Tathāgata Padmagarbha, he joined his palms in reverence and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
“Furthermore, if there is a person who can merely join their palms, prostrate, and pay respectful homage to this True Dharma, what kind of virtuous benefit will they obtain?
The Buddha said to Puyong:

“The mass of merit obtained by such a person is likewise boundless. It is like the Lake Anavatapta, the abode of the Naga King, where the palaces are not reached by the sun’s rays; from it flow five great rivers, and the water never runs dry.”
"Suppose there were a person who wished to know the number of drops in a pool of water, drop by drop. Do you think such a person would be able to know it?
Pu Yong replied, "No."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said,
“The roots of goodness possessed by this True Dharma of the Great Assembly are likewise vast and beyond compare.”
Even if someone were to wish to know the measure of the merit of this Dharma, they could not exhaust it even after passing through a thousand kalpas.
Furthermore, Universal Valor!

This Dharma is profound, difficult to understand, and difficult to realize; it is that which all Tathāgatas together revere. If there should be anyone who listens to and receives it for even a moment, they will immediately obtain such vast benefit.
The Bodhisattva Samantavīra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What are the names of those five great rivers?"
The Buddha said:
"The five great rivers are as follows:
the Gaṅgā River, the Sindhu River, the Vakṣu River, the Yamunā River, and the Sarabhū River."
Each of these five great rivers is surrounded by five hundred minor rivers, all of which flow and pour into the great ocean. Within each of these five great rivers dwells a great nāga king:
namely, the Nāga King Nanda, the Nāga King Śaṅkha, the Nāga King Vāhanī, the Nāga King Citrāsena, and the Nāga King Dharmacintin.

These and other such nāga kings, each accompanied by a retinue of one thousand, send down timely sweet rain upon Jambudvīpa. Consequently, the hundred grains and all crops flourish and grow; even the mountains, rivers, ravines, forests, thickets, springs, and ponds—down to the flowers, fruits, gourds, branches, leaves, roots, and stalks—wherever the rain falls, there is nothing that is not abundant and sufficient.

"Samantavīra, you should know that if there are sentient beings who, regarding this true Dharma, give rise to unwholesome verbal karma and produce disparaging slanders, the transgression they incur will be immeasurable and boundless."

Furthermore, if there are sentient beings who, regarding this True Dharma, give rise to virtuous verbal karma and offer praise, the mass of merit they obtain will likewise be immeasurable and boundless. Such a person will be able to draw near to spiritual friends and behold the Tathāgata; if they behold the Buddha, they will be able to eliminate all karmic obstructions and hindrances.
“Samantavīra!
It is like a Wheel-Turning King of Iron among the four great continents who rules over one continent; he is majestic, sovereign, vast, and blissful, and is further able to benefit all the people.”
This True Dharma of the present great assembly is likewise so: within Jambudvīpa, it brings great benefit to all sentient beings.

If one does not hear this True Dharma, that person will be unable to achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; they will be unable to abide at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), occupy the lion throne, turn the great wheel of Dharma, or beat the great drum of Dharma; nor will they be able to enter the realm of *nirvāṇa* or emit great radiance that universally illumines the world.
The Bodhisattva Samantavīra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Regarding the seers spoken of by the Tathāgata Padmagarbha in that world, Padmottara, who are able to cause those who have committed the five heinous acts to extinguish their grave offenses—I truly do not know at what stage they abide. I pray that the Buddha, out of his great compassion, will explain this for me.”
The Buddha said to Samantavīra:
“That seer has already attained the stage of non-retrogression and has long since accomplished the True Dharma of the Great Assembly.

Samantavīra, you should know that the speech of the Buddhas is profoundly deep and subtle. If there are those who, upon hearing this True Dharma, give rise to profound faith and acceptance, they shall see that seer; they shall likewise see the exquisite physical marks of as many Tathāgatas, Buddhas, as there are grains of sand in the Ganges. These beings will be loved and respected by the Buddhas, praised by the Buddhas, and will always dwell securely in the samādhis of the Buddhas, being able to penetrate such a True Dharma of the Great Assembly.”
