At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Samantavīra, saying:
"Listen attentively now."
I recall that in the past, immeasurable, incalculable, and asankhyeya kalpas ago, I encountered twelve koṭis of Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, all bearing the same name, Ratnottama.

At that time, I practiced the perfection of giving; I made offerings to each of those Buddhas with food and drink, clothing, exquisite ornaments, rare jewels, necklaces, as well as various flower garlands, ointments, and perfumes.
At that time, all those Tathāgatas bestowed upon me the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Universal Courage!
I further recall that in a past kalpa, I encountered eighteen koṭis of Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyak-saṃbuddhas, all bearing the same name, Ratnaprabha."

At that time, I also practiced the conduct of heroic giving, and with the aforementioned various offerings and requisites, I made offerings to each and every one of those Buddhas; at that time, all those Tathāgatas also conferred upon me the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Universal Courage!
Furthermore, I recall that in a past kalpa, I encountered twenty koṭis of Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, all bearing the same name, Śikhi.”

At that time, I also practiced the conduct of heroic giving and likewise made offerings to each of those Buddhas with the aforementioned articles of worship; at that time, all those Tathāgatas also bestowed upon me the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Universal Courage!
I further recall that in a past kalpa, I encountered twenty koṭis of Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, all bearing the same name Kāśyapa.

At that time, I also practiced the giving of heroic deeds, and with the aforementioned various offerings and requisites, I made offerings to each and every one of those Buddhas; at that time, all those Tathāgatas also conferred upon me the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Universal Valor!
I further recall that in a past kalpa, I encountered sixteen koṭis of Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, all bearing the same name, Vimalaprabha.”

At that time, I also practiced the conduct of heroic giving as a great elder of immense wealth; with the aforementioned various offerings and requisites, I made offerings to each and every one of those Buddhas, and at that time, all those Tathāgatas likewise bestowed upon me the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Universal Courage!
I further recall that in a past kalpa, I encountered ninety-five koṭis of Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, all bearing the same name, Śāntamati.

At that time, I also practiced the conduct of heroic giving as a great king; I was able to govern all with the True Dharma, enjoying sovereign happiness and immeasurable worldly wealth. With the aforementioned various offerings and requisites, I made individual offerings to each of those Buddhas, and at that time, all those Tathāgatas likewise bestowed upon me the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Samantavīra! Furthermore, I recall that in a past kalpa, I encountered ninety koṭis of Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, all bearing the same name, Vyūha.”

At that time, I was also practicing the conduct of heroic giving; as a brāhmaṇa possessing a great accumulation of treasures, I gave away all my possessions at once and prepared the aforementioned various exquisite offerings, making offerings to each of those Buddhas one by one. At that time, all those Tathāgatas likewise bestowed upon me the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Universal Hero!
Furthermore, I recall that in a past kalpa, I encountered eighteen koṭis of Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, all bearing the same name, Kanakamuni.”

At that time, I also practiced the conduct of heroic giving, and with the aforementioned various offerings and requisites, I made offerings to each and every one of those Buddhas; at that time, all those Tathāgatas also conferred upon me the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Samantavīra! I further recall that in a past kalpa, I encountered thirteen koṭis of Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, all bearing the same name Śrīprabha.”

At that time, I also practiced the giving of heroic deeds and likewise made offerings to each of those Buddhas with the aforementioned articles of worship; at that time, all those Tathāgatas also conferred upon me the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Universal Valor!
I further recall that in a past kalpa, I encountered twenty-five koṭis of Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, all bearing the same name, ‘Exquisite Flower.’”

At that time, I first gave rise to the mind of faith, left the household life to cultivate the Way, and constantly practiced with diligence; toward each and every one of these Tathāgatas, I served, honored, and made offerings with reverence, no differently than Ānanda did.
At that time, all those Tathāgatas likewise bestowed upon me the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Universal Valor!
I further recall that in a past kalpa, I encountered twelve koṭis of Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyak-saṃbuddhas, all bearing the same name, Vijaya-darśana."
At that time, I also renounced the household life there.

At that time, all sentient beings within Jambudvīpa were exceedingly wealthy, fully possessed of the seven treasures, and enjoyed unhindered happiness; not a single sentient being suffered from the pain of insufficiency.
When those Buddhas appeared in the world, they extensively proclaimed the True Dharma of the Great Assembly for the sake of sentient beings.
At that time, I paid homage to, revered, served, and made offerings to those Tathāgatas, seeking from them the prediction of my attainment of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, none of those Buddhas conferred a prediction of enlightenment upon me.
I then addressed them, saying:
"O Buddhas, World-Honored Ones!"
"When shall I receive the prediction of enlightenment?
Those Buddhas replied,
"O son of good family!"
"After you have passed this incalculable eon (asaṃkhyeya-kalpa), a Buddha will appear in the world named Dīpaṃkara; that Blessed One shall bestow upon you the prediction of enlightenment.
Having heard these words of the Buddhas at that time, I cultivated the bodhisattva practices with even greater diligence.

Immediately thereafter, after another incalculable eon (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) had passed, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara appeared in the world; at that time, I was a young brahmin (*māṇavaka*) named Jayamegha.

Having practiced the various holy life (brahmacarya), he was able to see that Buddha; filled with great joy, he paid him respectful homage and veneration, conceiving a sense of rare wonder. He then took seven stalks of *utpala* flowers and offered them to that Buddha, making this aspiration:
"By means of these roots of goodness, may I dedicate them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
At that time, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, amidst the great assembly, bestowed upon me this prediction, saying:
"O son of good family!
In a future age, after incalculable kalpas have passed, you shall attain Buddhahood and be named Śākyamuni, fully endowed with the ten titles."

At that time, having received the prophecy, I leaped into the air before that Buddha to a height of twelve tāla trees; then, returning to the ground, with a single-minded joy, I immediately realized the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).

“Samantavīra, you should know that throughout these countless kalpas, my cultivation of all pure conduct, my planting of all roots of goodness, and my making offerings to all Buddhas were all for the sake of fulfilling the various pāramitās;
having fulfilled them myself, I have further caused countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of sentient beings to likewise fulfill all such dharmas of the pāramitās.”
Today, I have already attained the realization of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and shall extensively proclaim for all sentient beings this most supreme, profound, and subtle Dharma-gate.
If there are sentient beings who delight in seeing the Buddhas, he immediately manifests a Buddha-body and preaches the Dharma for them;
if there are sentient beings who delight in seeing Bodhisattvas, he immediately manifests a Bodhisattva-body and preaches the Dharma for them;
if there are sentient beings who delight in seeing Pratyekabuddhas, he immediately manifests a Pratyekabuddha-body and preaches the Dharma for them.
If there are sentient beings who delight in seeing Śrāvakas, he immediately manifests the body of a Śrāvaka and preaches the Dharma for them.
Furthermore, if they are in the realm of gods, he immediately manifests a celestial body and preaches the Dharma for them;
if they are in the realm of humans, he immediately manifests a human body and preaches the Dharma for them.
If they are in the realm of dragons, he manifests in the form of a dragon and preaches the Dharma for them;
if they are in the realm of yakṣas, he manifests in the form of a yakṣa and preaches the Dharma for them;
if they are in the realm of hungry ghosts, he manifests in their form and preaches the Dharma for them.

Manifesting bodies according to the various forms and appearances of all sentient beings throughout the realms of existence, he proclaims the sublime Dharma through skillful means, causing them to be free from fear and to attain deep faith and understanding.
“Universal Courage!
For what reason do I now employ various skillful means to manifest in diverse forms and preach the Dharma?

It is so that when sentient beings hear this Dharma, they may attain the great dhāraṇī of ultimate truth; they may contemplate all worlds with the perception of impermanence; they may constantly mindfully practice all wholesome dharmas; and they may ultimately become free from all defilements, such that their true roots of goodness are never diminished.”
Throughout the long night, I have used these skillful means to benefit, bring peace, and bring happiness to all sentient beings.
Universal Valor!
As I have said above, this True Dharma of the Great Assembly possesses such merit as this.
Among those in this assembly, some who had given rise to doubt said to one another:
"Does the karmic fruit of the True Dharma exist,
or does it not exist?"
Is Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi attainable, or is it unattainable?
Are all sentient beings able to be delivered?
"Is it because they cannot be delivered? Some spoke thus:
"As the Buddha has taught, all phenomena truly have causes that can produce effects, and effects must necessarily arise from causes."
"For one who plants the seeds of wholesome causes, what could be lost of wholesome dharmas? Others spoke thus:
"All dharmas do not exist; even their karmic retribution does not exist."
"Since the cause is fundamentally empty from the beginning, how could there be a fruit?
Since both cause and fruit do not exist, talk of a destination is but false speech.
Thus spoke Puyong!
The mental activities of all sentient beings differ, with light and darkness being mutually opposed and causes and effects naturally distinct.
One who correctly explains this gives rise to the vision of reality; this is precisely what is called the establishment of the True Dharma.
Listen now as I describe this person’s karmic reward: for twenty kalpas they shall not be born in Uttarakuru;
for twenty-five kalpas they shall be born exclusively in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;

when their retribution in that heaven is exhausted, they shall be born within hundreds of thousands of Buddha-fields, where they shall behold those Buddhas and hear the True Dharma. Such a person shall never again regress from Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Those who propagate such false teachings give rise to the view of annihilationism; this is precisely what is called "destroying the True Dharma.
Listen now further to the retribution for this person's sin: after his life here ends, he will be born in the Great Hell to suffer for one kalpa;
in this manner, for eight full kalpas—one kalpa after another—he will be born individually in each of the great hells.

Having undergone such great suffering in these eight great hells, they will continue to be reborn in turn within the three evil realms for nine thousand and twenty-eight kalpas, enduring great anguish and distress.
Once these kalpas have passed, although they may obtain a human body, for sixteen thousand kalpas they shall die while still in the womb;
and for fourteen thousand kalpas, their tongue-faculty shall be incomplete.
For twelve thousand kalpas, he was Maṃsabhinna;
for eleven thousand kalpas, he was born blind from birth.

"Puyong, you should know that all sentient beings are inexhaustible. Whether in this realm or another realm, whether through conditions of birth or death, whether in appropriate or inappropriate places, whether agreeable or disagreeable—all are fashioned by the mind alone and manifest according to karma."
There are some sentient beings who, by practicing various wholesome dharmas, attain birth in the celestial realms;
there are some sentient beings who, for the sake of bodhi, cultivate various practices and vows;
and there are some sentient beings who gradually attain ultimate, unsurpassed quiescence.

For this reason, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, for the sake of countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of sentient beings—whether they have already set out on the path or have not yet set out, whether they be devas, humans, nāgas, spirits, or others—preach the Dharma to transform and deliver them without ceasing for even a single kṣaṇa.

At that time, while the World-Honored One was preaching the Dharma, there were another eighty-four thousand assemblies of brahmins and ninety thousand koṭis of non-Buddhist followers, such as the Nirgranthas, who deliberated among themselves, saying:
"Now, the śramaṇa Gautama resides on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha; what is he teaching to this great assembly gathered here?"
"Let us now go together to him and engage in debate!
At that very moment, after the various Brahmins and non-Buddhists had thus deliberated among themselves, they approached the Buddha's dwelling accompanied by countless followers.
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately emitted a great, rare, pure, and wondrous radiance from within the assembly, illuminating the entire multitude.
Then, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"This light was not emitted without cause or condition.
Now this great assembly all desires to hear and know [the reason]; we pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will explain it for us.
The Buddha said:
“Good son! You should now know that there are immeasurable multitudes gathered here in this assembly.
Maitreya Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what kind of assembly?
Is it for the assembly of devas?”
"Is it an assembly of humans?
Or an assembly of nāgas, devas, yakṣas, and so forth?
The Buddha said to Maitreya:
"As you have said, all have assembled here; furthermore, there are various Brahmins, non-Buddhists, Nirgranthas, and other groups who have entered this assembly to debate with me."

Once they have been tamed, I shall immediately preach the Dharma to them as is appropriate; those eighty-four thousand brahmins, ninety thousand koṭis of non-Buddhist followers, Nirgranthas, and the rest of the assembly will all resolve their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Maitreya! Furthermore, there were eighteen thousand koṭis of nāga kings who entered this assembly; having heard me preach the Dharma, they too all resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Furthermore, sixty thousand koṭis of the assembly of Śuddhaprabha devaputras, thirty-two thousand koṭis of the assembly of all celestial Māra hosts, and twelve thousand koṭis of the assembly of asuras—all such beings as these came to enter the assembly to listen to and receive the True Dharma.
Furthermore, there were great kings, namely:

King Joyful, King Wondrous Joy, King Supreme Joy, King Human Sage, King Pure Army, King Brahma Sound, King Good Appearance, King Beloved Army, King Joyful Army, King Wondrous Color, King Victorious Army, and King Increasing; these and others, five hundred great kings in total, each accompanied by a retinue of a thousand koṭis, all came to enter the assembly to hear and receive the True Dharma, and each remained steadfast in their resolve for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“Maitreya! It is for these reasons that I emit this radiance.

At that time, when the Bodhisattva Maitreya heard the Buddha speak thus regarding this great assembly—among the devas, humans, non-humans, and others—seeing those who had resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and those who, having heard the True Dharma, gave rise to faith and acceptance, he was filled with great joy. Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and circumambulated him three times to the right, he immediately vanished from the midst of the assembly, his body no longer visible.

At that time, the various brahmins, non-Buddhist practitioners, nirgranthas, jainas, and pāśupatas, as well as devas, nāgas, and even the five hundred great kings, having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, paid their respects according to their respective customs and each sat to one side.
At that time, there were thirty thousand koṭis of great bodhisattvas in the eastern direction, and likewise in the southeastern direction;
fifty thousand koṭis of great bodhisattvas in the southern direction, and likewise in the southwestern direction;
sixty thousand koṭis of great bodhisattvas in the western direction, and likewise in the northwestern direction.

In the north there were eighty thousand koṭis of great bodhisattvas; in the northeast it was likewise. In the zenith there were one hundred thousand koṭis of great bodhisattvas, and in the nadir there were ninety thousand koṭis of great bodhisattvas. Such great assemblies of bodhisattvas from the ten directions—all of whom had already perfected the ten stages—came from their respective quarters into the Buddha’s assembly. Having arrived at the Buddha’s presence, each bowed his head at the World-Honored One’s feet in salutation and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Samantavīra, saying: "Samantavīra!
You should now once again go to the worlds of the ten directions and proclaim to the assemblies of bodhisattvas, speaking these words:"
"Today the Tathāgata shall proclaim the True Dharma of the Great Assembly for the sake of all sentient beings," he said,
causing all the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions to join their palms in prostration at his crown and give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Samantavīra, having received the holy command of the Buddha, prostrated with his head at the feet of the World-Honored One, circumambulated him three times to the right, and suddenly vanished from the assembly. He traveled throughout the worlds of the ten directions, and in each direction, he raised a great voice and proclaimed:
"In this Sahā world, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni shall now proclaim the True Dharma of the Great Assembly for the sake of all sentient beings!"
Thus, repeating this three times, they all proclaimed these words:
"Now, in this Sahā world, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni shall proclaim the True Dharma of the Great Assembly for the sake of sentient beings!"
At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions and all the Bodhisattvas, hearing these words, each praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
Śākyamuni Tathāgata, you are able to bestow benefit and peace upon sentient beings."
He also praised the Bodhisattva Samantavīra, who is able to proclaim the Buddha’s work throughout the worlds of the ten directions.

At that time, after the Bodhisattva Samantavīra had everywhere in the worlds of the ten directions proclaimed this to the great Bodhisattvas, he returned to this land in the blink of an eye. Standing before the Buddha, he prostrated at the World-Honored One’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, four Wind Deity Kings arrived from the four directions and entered the assembly; they purified the entire realm of Rājagṛha for more than a hundred yojanas, making it entirely free of dust and impurities.
Śakra-devendra entered the assembly holding his vajra; all the māras and non-Buddhists gazed upon him with trepidation.

Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, great clouds of incense spread through the void and a great rain of fragrance fell, such that even aloeswood and sandalwood could not serve as a metaphor for its excellence.
Furthermore, a rain of various celestial flowers fell, namely:
Utpala flowers, kumuda flowers, puṇḍarīka flowers, and various other exquisite blossoms remained suspended in the air and transformed into parasols;

furthermore, above the Buddha, eighty-four thousand pavilions were manifested, each fashioned from the seven precious gems and adorned with a multitude of variegated colors in most wonderful splendor.
Furthermore, within the sky, immeasurable and boundless great jewel thrones appeared; upon each throne there was a Buddha, manifesting to proclaim the sublime Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
At that time, this trichiliocosm shook in six ways. Then,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantavīra joined his palms in reverence and addressed the Buddha, saying,
“World-Honored One!
For what cause and condition has this auspicious sign appeared in the void? It is truly rare.
Furthermore, this great earth has suddenly trembled; we pray that the Buddha, out of his compassion, will explain this for us.
The Buddha said to Samantavīra:
"Now, all the great bodhisattvas from the ten directions, as well as devas, humans, nāgas, spirits, and others, have gathered here in this assembly; I shall now proclaim the True Dharma for them."
Furthermore, for the sake of all non-Buddhists, in order to shatter their deviant minds and cause them to return to right view, he manifests this auspicious omen for these reasons.

Universal Valor, you should know that although ordinary beings may encounter a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha appearing in the world, they are unable to give rise to a mind of reverence toward the Buddha’s sublime physical marks, nor do they conceive the thought that such an encounter is difficult to find. Even if they hear the Buddha proclaim the True Dharma, they are unable to practice according to the Dharma; instead, they grasp at signs and give rise to a mind of pride. Having heard it but briefly, they falsely produce many interpretations and further conceive the notion that it is easily obtained. Thus, they harbor doubts and lack faith, speaking as follows:

"As the Buddha has taught, whether in the sūtras or in the geyas, there is that which I have not previously heard or known; I am currently unable to listen to, receive, or remember it, yet I fully understand all dharmas for myself."

Because this person possesses such a deluded mind, they indulge their own ignorance and turn their back on the Buddha-dharma. They create the causes for sinful karma by composing their own scriptures and compiling their own doctrines, proclaiming them as the correct teaching within the world, and saying:
"What I have composed and compiled is skillful wisdom; I shall further exhort others to practice it."

"Even though he encourages others to practice by means of the scriptures he himself has composed, despite employing various skillful means, he is ultimately unable to cause even a single *pudgala* to obtain benefit and happiness; instead, throughout many lifetimes, he ruins his own body."
Due to the causes and conditions of their karma, at the time of death they will undergo great suffering and affliction.
"Universal Courage!

These non-Buddhists give rise to deluded minds and produce false views; they cannot attain liberation. It is like fledglings that have just been born: as long as their wings and feathers have not yet grown, how could they possibly fly?"
To say that they can fly is a falsehood!
Unless these followers of external paths turn their minds toward the Buddha’s True Dharma, how could they ever attain ultimate, unsurpassed, and pure nirvana?
That they constantly reckon themselves to have attained nirvāṇa is likewise false and deceptive!

Why is this? These followers of external paths create improper causes and give rise to the grasping of precepts and observances; they destroy their own persons, sever the true Dharma, and are stubbornly attached to the view of self, having no means by which to achieve liberation.
Even having obtained a human body is not yet a superior retribution; how, then, could one truly attain pure nirvana?
Regarding one's own person, one has not yet even known from where it originally came.
Where will they go?
Their births and deaths are in vain; they undergo all manner of suffering and affliction, increasing their rebirths in the evil realms without respite.
As I observe these beings, I feel deep compassion for them.
At that time, having spoken thus, the World-Honored One addressed the various non-Buddhists, Nirgranthas, and others, saying:
"You should know that within Jambudvīpa there is a great treasure which no one can protect; you may use it as you please."
This great collection of Dharma that I have proclaimed, I do not withhold from anyone who seeks it.
If you have any doubts or anything you wish to inquire about, feel free to ask; out of great compassion, the Tathāgata will explain and reveal each point to you individually.
At that time, the various non-Buddhists, including the Nirgranthas, each rose from their seats, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and addressed him with these words:
"World-Honored One!

The Buddha, throughout the long night, has delivered all sentient beings, causing them to emerge from saṃsāra; how is it that these sentient beings continue in a succession of birth and death without interruption?
Regarding this matter, I am unable to fully comprehend it.
“I pray that the Buddha will proclaim it.
At that time, the World-Honored One, within the assembly, addressed the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja-sena, saying:

“Now, because these various followers of external paths within this assembly have been illuminated by the majestic spiritual power and the light of my Great Dharma, they are gradually able to attain understanding and insight. Having donned the armor of diligence and stilled their hearts of doubt, they are able to inquire of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, regarding this meaning.”
Bhaiṣajyarāja!
All those who are born are, in brief, of two kinds:
first, those who have been born for a long time; second, those who are newly born.

For example, suppose there is a person of great wealth and power who, at one time, washes his hair with water and adorns himself with fresh, clean, and exquisite garments before departing from his house.
At that time, there was a poor man who, upon seeing this, felt great joy. He immediately returned home, bathed his own hair, and washed his old clothes with the water to make them clean.
Although this man drew much water and washed those old garments, he merely exhausted himself; in the end, he could not make his clothing look new or fine.
Among all births, those who have been born for a long time are like that poor man who washes his old clothes; they can never be made clean.
Those who are newly born are like that wealthy man wearing new, fine garments, upon which no dust or grime has yet settled.
At that time, the various brahmins, non-Buddhist ascetics, Nirgranthas, and others, having heard these words spoken by the Buddha, addressed him, saying:
"What is it that is first born?"
"What is meant by 'long-lived'?
The Buddha said, "Among those in the six realms of existence, sentient beings who undergo suffering through continuous succession are called long-lived. Why is this so?"
"These sentient beings, within the six realms of existence, do not give rise to weary detachment nor do they seek liberation.
At that time, the various brahmins, non-Buddhists, and others again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
As the Buddha has taught, sentient beings who have been born for a long time within saṃsāra undergo various sufferings and afflictions and are unable to attain liberation.
May the Buddha reveal [the path] for those sentient beings who are newly born.

After these words had been spoken, at that moment, ninety-four thousand koṭis of mānavakas suddenly entered the assembly; they stood silently before the World-Honored One, neither prostrating in salutation nor asking any questions.
At that time, having witnessed this event, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja addressed the Buddha,
saying: "World-Honored One,
for what cause and condition have these individuals now entered the Buddha’s assembly, yet neither pay homage nor put forward any questions?"
"What is the matter with them?
The Buddha said to Bhaisajyasena, "These māṇavakas are but newly born; they have not yet had occasion to question the Buddha, the World-Honored One."
At that time, those māṇavakas spoke thus:
“World-Honored One!
We are those who have been born for the first time.”
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is!
When you were first born, you were like the rising sun; your radiance shone universally upon all things, and you were gazed upon by immeasurable sentient beings."

For a long time you have been on the Buddha-way, and your minds are already matured; you have long since mastered all the dharmas of the bodhisattvas, so that although you are called "newly born," you have practiced for a long time.
At that time, ninety-four thousand koṭis of newborn maṇḍalika youths each leaped into the air and descended from mid-air, and every one of them attained the perfection of the tenth bhūmi.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja joined his palms in reverent salutation, gave rise to a sense of rare wonder, and stepped forward to address the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!

These sentient beings have attained great and excellent benefit; they have long since exhausted the suffering and affliction of saṃsāra and possess great vigor. They are called 'newly born,' yet today, upon seeing the Buddha, they have attained liberation in a single kṣaṇa."

At that time, among the assembly of Brahmins, non-Buddhists, Nirgranthas, and others, there were those who were blind; by virtue of hearing the Dharma, they suddenly beheld a brilliant light and each was able to perceive the Buddha’s exquisite and wondrous physical marks.
Having beheld the marks of the Buddha, they all spoke these words:
"The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is the most supreme teacher; we take refuge in him!"
They immediately rose, joined their palms, gave rise to pure faith, and together addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We have now been granted the sight of the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"You should once again examine with careful discernment the sublime and excellent physical marks of the Buddha-Tathāgata.

You should know this: because the power of your various roots of goodness has now matured, you have been able to see the World-Honored One and have also been able to hear the Dharma of the Great Assembly."
At that time, the blind followers of external paths, having received this benefit, were filled with great joy; each of them resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

At that time, the various brahmins, non-Buddhists, nirgranthas, and others in the assembly, having heard the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma, also all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. They realized the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena) and fully perfected the ten stages (*bhūmi*). Immediately, they became a great assembly of *mahāsattva* bodhisattvas. Thereupon, each leaped into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees, and while in mid-air, each manifested various supernatural transformations and emanated diverse flower garlands, necklaces, parasols, banners, pennants, and pavilions made of the seven precious jewels.

Remaining above the Buddha, they made offerings to him, each thinking: "Now this body of mine is born from the Buddha's wisdom and born from the True Dharma; all Tathāgatas are the true place of refuge."
Having formed this thought, he descended from the air, prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, there were countless hundreds of thousands of devaputras in the assembly who, having witnessed this event, immediately spoke these verses:
"Our Buddha, the Great Śramaṇa, Has attained the most supreme and excellent benefit."
In all the worlds, you are most honored and without equal.
Your samādhis and the power of your vows are entirely perfected;
regarding all dharmas of ultimate meaning, there is nothing you do not know.
All classes of sentient beings, suffering in the beginningless cycle of saṃsāra,
are universally enabled to attain liberation through the Buddha’s skillful means;
even the Brahmins and non-Buddhists all obtain great benefit and joy.
The Sūtra of the True Dharma of the Great Assembly Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Three.
The Sūtra of the True Dharma of the Great Assembly Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Four.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja-kumāra rose from his seat, increased his reverence, knelt with his knees touching the ground, and prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One. Having prostrated, he joined his palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
“By what causes and conditions are these bodhisattvas able to manifest various supernatural transformations in mid-air and manifest various forms before the Tathāgata?
The Buddha said,
“Listen attentively!”

Bhaiṣajyasena! These sons of good family have already been collectively sustained by all the Tathāgatas; before long, they will attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, occupy the great Dharma throne, and turn the wondrous wheel of Dharma. With the radiance of the Dharma, they will universally illumine all classes of beings. By these causes and conditions, they are able to manifest transformations.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, since the Buddha has, throughout the long night, liberated all sentient beings within the triple world in such vast numbers, how is it that they have no end?”
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent, Bhaiṣajyarāja!
It is, for example, like a person who sows various kinds of grain and wheat, keeping each distinct and unmixed.
Subsequently, when the time comes, all those seeds reach full maturity.
This person immediately gathers [the grain] in succession; whether it be rice or wheat, there is no intermingling.
Thus, having gathered it in turn, he sows it again; having sown it, he gathers it again, without end.
Bhaiṣajyarāja!
These sentient beings are also like this: by reason of their karmic causes and conditions, they sow various seeds, whether wholesome or unwholesome, without any intermingling.
When they ripen at a later time, they will experience their various karmic retributions without any intermingling.
In this manner, proceeding by succession, birth follows birth without end. "Bhaiṣajyarāja!
All those who practice the bodhisattva path are able to sow the seeds of all wholesome dharmas, bringing each one to maturity;
once matured, they are able to give rise to all wholesome dharmas;
and once these wholesome dharmas have arisen, they experience great joy and come to cherish and delight in the Buddha-dharma.
Those seeds of wholesome dharmas, though they pass through many kalpas, can never be destroyed.

Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that this is called a bodhisattva who has first resolved on awakening; all the wholesome dharmas he has attained he gathers and fully understands, and they increase and become ever more excellent. Even when he sees things in a dream, he is able to remain free from all fears.

Why is this? Because all karmic obstructions have been completely purified; they do not create unwholesome dharmas and are free from all suffering and affliction, such that even when adverse conditions appear before them, they cannot be moved.
If, within a dream, one sees a great mass of fire with blazing and intense flames,
the bodhisattva, having seen it, does not give rise to fear. Why is this?
The firewood of all afflictions is consumed by the fire of wisdom, such that nothing can disturb it.
Furthermore, if one sees great water in a dream that is not clean, but is turbid and foul to its very depths.
Having seen this, the bodhisattva likewise does not give rise to fear. Why is this?
Because he has exhausted all karmic actions, he attains mastery like an ox that has shed its yoke.
Furthermore, even in a dream, one might take a sharp sword and sever one's own head, or sever the heads of others;
at that time, the bodhisattva likewise gives rise to no fear.
Why is this? Because among all afflictions, greed, hatred, and delusion constitute the root; since the Bodhisattva has already severed them, he has nothing to fear.
Bhaiṣajyarāja!

Although that bodhisattva who has first resolved on awakening has already attained liberation from the saṃsāra of the six destinies, he nevertheless takes birth therein in accordance with conditions; all of this is the bodhisattva’s manifestation through the power of skillful means to transform and deliver all sentient beings. In reality, however, the bodhisattva is always born within the pure lands of all Buddhas, being collectively sustained by all Tathāgatas.

“Bhaiṣajyasena! You should know now that if, in the future final age, there are sentient beings who are able to give rise to the mind of dedication toward Bodhi, they will thereby abide in the wisdom of all Buddhas, attain the vision of the perfect and wholesome dharmas of all Buddhas, and never again give rise to a mind of doubt.”
Bhaiṣajyarāja!

For countless hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kalpas, I diligently practiced austerities and cultivated all wholesome dharmas; having awakened to the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, I attained the realization of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Having thus perfected these, he further employs skillful means and wise discernment to extensively expound all dharmas, enabling all sentient beings to be born within the pure lands of the Buddhas and experience supreme, wondrous bliss. Therein, they are able to understand the dharmas of cessation and the path; they understand the supreme, wondrous fundamental dharmas; they understand the supreme, wondrous dharmas of the wholesome realms; they understand the supreme, wondrous dharmas of supernormal powers; and they understand the supreme, wondrous dharmas of the tranquility of the wholesome realms.
“Bhaiṣajyarāja!
As for what is called ‘extinction,’ what is its meaning?
Bhaiṣajyasena Bodhisattva replied:
“World-Honored One!
What is meant by the ‘sphere of phenomena’ (dharmāyatana)? The Buddha said:
“What is the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana)?
The Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja said:

“As for that sphere of phenomena, it refers to the two dharmas of diligence and ethical discipline. Whether they have already been initiated or not yet initiated, the perfection of ethical conduct is called the treasury of phenomena.”
“World-Honored One!
All dharmas are born from this treasury of Dharma.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent, Bhaiṣajyarāja!
You are able to answer this meaning in the presence of the Tathāgata.”
The Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what purpose do the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, appear in the world?”
The Buddha said to Bhaiṣajyarāja:

“The appearance of the Buddhas in the world is for the purpose of causing all sentient beings to fulfill their observance of the precepts and their great learning; to cause them to fully understand the place of supreme and wondrous bliss; and to cause them to penetrate and enter into all supreme and wondrous Dharma-gates. Having entered these Dharma-gates, they are then able to extensively cultivate all wholesome dharmas, increasing their roots of goodness through the power of skillful means, and attaining complete penetration of both mundane and supramundane, most supreme and wondrous dharmas.”
The Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja said to the Buddha,
“World-Honored One,
what is called the supramundane dharma?”
The Buddha said to Bhaiṣajyarāja:
“The supramundane dharma is what is called the dharma of nirvāṇa; if one thoroughly understands the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, that is precisely to understand the supreme dharma of nirvāṇa.”

Those dharmas are the aggregate of the True Dharma (*saddharmaskandha*); if one knows these dharmas as they truly are and realizes them as they truly are, this is the foremost among supramundane dharmas.

Bhaiṣajyasena! Those ordinary beings who, amidst the profound and subtle Dharma of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, do not themselves give rise to faith, incline toward it, or practice it, and furthermore cannot encourage others to do so—when these ordinary beings' bodies perish and their lives end, they have no wholesome dharmas to rely upon as their refuge.
"Bhaiṣajyasena! Listen attentively now.
I recall that in the past there was a merchant who, for the sake of seeking profit, borrowed a thousand ounces of gold and intended to go to another country to engage in trade."
Out of affection for their son, his parents said to him:

"These gold and treasures do not belong to you; if you carry them away yourself, they may be lost at some point, causing your suffering and distress to increase tenfold—what benefit would there be in such regret?"
At that time, the son instead gave rise to resentment and did not heed these words; he immediately took up the gold and departed for another country.

Once he arrived there, before long, all the gold he carried was lost and ruined, and he gained nothing at all. Gradually unable to remain there, he immediately felt regret and was overcome with great anguish.
At a later time, although that man returned to his country, he did not go home; with a heart of suffering and distress, he fell gravely ill.

At that time, his parents knew that although their son had returned, he had not yet gone home. Furthermore, hearing that all the gold and treasures had been dissipated and ruined, they were filled with grief and confusion, and said to one another in secret:
"This is not our son; he is a great evil friend who has destroyed our clan, reduced us all to poverty, and brought further enmity upon us. Upon whom can we rely?"
"What skillful means can we now employ to escape this suffering?
At that time, because of their grief and anguish, the parents grew weary of their own lives and desired to bring about their own deaths.
At that time, having heard that his parents were so distressed, the merchant immediately returned home and stood before them, choking with emotion.
When his parents suddenly saw their son, they instantly cast aside their previous anger and said to him together:
"My son, how can you endure such suffering from this illness?"
"I heard of these matters and feared that you would pass away; now that you have come, you relieve my anxieties.
Then the merchant said to his parents:
"My body and mind are afflicted with such suffering, and my limbs are so tormented by pain that my life may not be saved."
For what reason?

At this moment, my eyes do not wish to see, my ears do not wish to hear, and my consciousness is bewildered and distressed; as all manner of sufferings converge, even if my parents were present, how could they protect me?
The parents said to him:
"My son, do not give rise to fear here; your life is not yet exhausted, and we shall protect you from all harm.
Your current suffering and distress must be due to a malignant fever that has caused your consciousness to become deluded and made you see things falsely."
At that time, the son replied:
"I am not afflicted by disease, nor do I see anything; all lovely objects do not appear before me, and I see only the suffering of death, a most terrifying thing."
"His destiny is fixed and he is about to die; no one can save him.

His parents replied, "The suffering of our son is likely caused by the possession of a celestial deity. All those in this world who are seized by such spirits go to the temples of the gods to seek protection; if you do so, only then will he be able to escape and be delivered."
The son said, "So be it.
At that time, his parents took exquisite incense and went at once to the celestial shrine.
Having arrived there, he informed the gatekeeper and was led before the deity to burn incense and offer prayers for repentance and forgiveness.
At that time, the gatekeeper said to the parents:
"If you wish for your son’s illness to be cured and the celestial deity to be pleased, you must perform a sacrificial offering; then you will surely obtain your heart's desire."
"As for the objects of sacrifice, according to the law one must take the life of one person and offer a bowl of dog meat; only then can it be called a sacrifice.
At that time, having heard those words, the parents said to each other:
"If we do not now perform this sacrifice to that celestial deity, by what means shall our son escape from this suffering?"
"However, my family is now in dire poverty; how can we afford the items required for that sacrifice?
We should return home together and devise some plan.
Having thus consulted with one another, they immediately returned home and, having exhausted everything they possessed, traded it all to obtain a single bowl of *śu*.
They then went out together from the house and approached a wealthy man, addressing him thus:
"We now seek to borrow a small portion of gold; we pledge to return it within ten days."
"If you violate these words and let more than ten days pass, I shall become your slave or servant with my very body.
Having spoken these words, the wealthy man immediately gave them to him.

At that time, having obtained the gold, the parents did not return home; instead, they took the gold and purchased a man. The man sold did not know what he was to do, so he followed his master to a celestial shrine.
Having arrived at the temple, he said to the gatekeeper:
"We have now come with sacrificial offerings to worship the celestial deity.
The gatekeeper replied:
"You may do as you wish.
Then, before the celestial deity, the parents burned incense and made this aspiration, saying:
"May our son be freed from the suffering of illness, and may the celestial deity be pleased."
Having spoken thus, he immediately took the person intended for sacrifice and the *bali* vessel, and with his own hands ended their lives to perform the offering.
At the moment the victim was being put to death, having been bound and restrained so that there was no way to escape, they could do nothing but keep the Buddhas in mind and uttered these words once:
"Namo Buddhāya! (Homage to the Buddha!)
Having spoken thus, his life came to an end.
Then that deva, having accepted the sacrifice, deceived the parents by saying:
"The illness from which your son suffered was seized by me; I have now released him, allowing your son to be delivered."
At that time, having heard these words, the parents leaped for joy and went out after bowing in thanks.
Celebrating together, they said to one another:

"Since our son has now recovered from his illness and will certainly attain a long life, although we have no gold to repay the wealthy man, we shall act according to our original promise and serve as his slaves and servants without any regret."
At that time, while the parents were still deliberating together and had not yet reached home, they suddenly encountered someone who informed them that their son’s life had come to an end.
Upon hearing these words, both parents were overcome with great anguish and collapsed to the ground, dying instantly.

The Buddha said to Bhaiṣajyasena, “I observe that the foolish ordinary beings of the world, entangled by delusion and karma, associate with unwholesome friends and gather together, mutually causing one another harm; it is just like this.”
"These ordinary beings, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, will fall into evil destinies and undergo great suffering and affliction; there is no one able to rescue or protect them.
The Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“Regarding those who perform sacrifices to the celestial deities as the Buddha has taught, where do these different types of beings fall after death?
The Buddha said to Bhaisajyasena, “Stop!”
"There is no need to ask.
The Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Among us there are those who wish to hear this; we pray that the Buddha will speak for them.
The Buddha said to Bhaiṣajyasena, "You should know this:
when those parents passed away, they both fell into the Saṃghāta Hell and underwent great suffering and affliction."
At that time, that son fell into the Saṃjīva (Reviving) Hell and underwent great suffering.
Because he had acted as a gatekeeper at that celestial shrine and had rejoiced in the guidance [of others], after his life ended, he fell into the Avīci Hell and underwent great suffering.
The Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Where will those persons who were sacrificed be reborn?”
The Buddha said to Bhaiṣajyarāja:
“This person, at the end of his life, will be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and experience supreme and wondrous bliss for sixty kalpas.
Bhaiṣajyarāja again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By what causes and conditions was this person able to be born there?
The Buddha said to Bhaiṣajyasena:

"When this person approaches the end of life, they will give rise to pure faith in accordance with pure goodness and take refuge in the Tathāgata. By reciting 'Namo Buddhāya' even once, this person shall plant profound roots of merit;
furthermore, for eighty kalpas, they will attain the knowledge of past lives, and in every place of rebirth, they will be free from all afflictions and have all suffering extinguished."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyasena came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For those sentient beings who desire to aspire toward and realize the dharma of nirvāṇa, what practice should they cultivate?”
The Buddha said to Bhaiṣajyarāja:
"You should cultivate the practice of diligent effort, being courageous and firm.
Bhaiṣajyarāja replied:
"What is called 'energetic practice' (vīrya-caryā)?
Furthermore, from what source can it be initiated?
The Buddha said:
“Those who practice with vigor do not slacken or retreat regarding the various fruits of the Dharma; this is called the practice of vigor. As for the bases of vigor, they are as follows:

the fruit of stream-entry is called a base of vigor; the fruit of once-returning is called a base of vigor; the fruit of non-returning is called a base of vigor; the fruit of arhatship is called a base of vigor; the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood and the fruit of the wisdom of a pratyekabuddha are called bases of vigor; and the fruit of bodhisattvahood and the fruit of the wisdom of a bodhisattva are called bases of vigor.”
"Bhaiṣajyasena! Those who cultivate awakening are able to give rise to vast diligence in such places as these.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyasena, saying:

"I recall that in the past, at one time, there was a māṇavaka who planted a single tree on level ground; immediately, its sprouts, stalks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits grew, glossy and lovely."
The roots of that tree spread out for one yojana, and all were fully formed in a mere moment.

Next, there was another māṇavaka who, beside the previous tree, also planted a tree; as soon as its roots touched the ground, it was suddenly uprooted and blown over by a great wind. Since even its sprouts, stems, branches, and leaves could not grow, how much less could its flowers and fruits ever come to fruition?
When the person who had planted the tree next to him saw this, he immediately moved that tree, intending to plant it elsewhere.
At that time, the person who had planted the tree first said:
"Why have you caused destruction upon my level and firm ground?"
The next person who had planted trees said, "I am now merely moving the trees I have planted myself; it is not that I am specifically destroying your level and firm ground!
Thus they went back and forth, contending with one another.
At that time, someone secretly informed the king.
Having heard this, the king issued an order to arrest them, and the messengers, obeying his command, rushed to that place.
Then, the two disputants were both greatly terrified as the messengers seized them and brought them before the king.
At that time, the king asked the two men,
"For what reason are you disputing with one another?
The man who had first planted the tree explained the matter exactly as it was.
Next, the tree-planter spoke these words:
"Great King, you should know that since I have no land of my own for planting, I have temporarily borrowed this person's land to plant trees."
That which I have planted has been uprooted by the wind; its roots cannot remain firm, and as for the sprouts, stalks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits, none of them can grow.
In a short time, this person planted trees that sprouted shoots and stems, fully endowed with branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit; furthermore, their roots spread out for a distance of one yojana.
Seeing this, I felt shame within myself and immediately moved the tree, intending to plant it elsewhere.

Having obtained what he desired, he became angry once more; for this reason, we have come to dispute with one another. I pray that Your Majesty will examine my case and not inflict punishment upon me.
Then, the king immediately issued an edict to assemble his ministers and officials.
At that time, there were thirty koṭis of such ministers and officials who, hearing the king’s command, all went together to the king's presence and said to him in unison:
"What decree do you proclaim?"

The king said, "You should know that a most rare event has just occurred within my kingdom: there is a man who, having planted but a single tree, saw it sprout roots and trunk, and fully develop branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit, all within a short time; furthermore, its roots have spread for a distance of one yojana. Have you ever seen such a thing before?"

"As I have observed, among all trees that flower and bear fruit with extreme rapidity, this occurs within half a month or at most one month. Yet this tree has never been seen or heard of before; what do you think of this?"
At that time, one among the ministers came forward and addressed the king, saying:

"Regarding this matter, I too have not yet reached a definitive conclusion as to its truth; I share the doubt you have expressed. I pray that Your Majesty will summon this tree-planter once more and question him thoroughly to ascertain whether it is so or not."
The king immediately summoned the man who had planted the tree and questioned him again:
"Is it true, as you have said, that the tree you planted blossomed and so forth within such a short time?"
"If you speak falsely, I shall surely punish you!
At that time, the man said:
"Your Majesty is like a parent who gave birth to me; how would I dare to speak falsely before Your Majesty?"
"I pray that Your Majesty will have no doubt; this matter is indeed true.
The king said, "I have never heard of such a thing before, much less have I ever seen it."
"How can I develop faith in this matter?
At that time, the man again addressed the king, saying:
"Great King, if you should still lack faith, I pray that Your Majesty will go there yourself to observe it."
Then the king, together with thirty koṭis of ministers, went to the place where the tree stood.
Having arrived there, he saw that the tree was lush with branches and leaves and abundant with fruit; having seen this, faith arose within him and he marveled at its rarity.
At that time, the king also planted a tree there, yet it likewise did not immediately produce sprouts, stems, branches, or leaves, much less flowers or fruit.
Having seen this, the king felt ashamed before his ministers and officials; overcome with great anger, he immediately issued an order to cut down the tree he had previously planted.
All the Mallas, obeying the king’s command, vied with one another to fell the trees with axes.
Yet, as each tree was being cut down, twelve trees would simultaneously spring up again, adorned with the seven treasures, vast and most exquisite.
When the king saw this, his anger flared up once more, and he again issued an order to cut down such trees as these.
Then, the Mallas together took up their axes and cut down twelve trees.
When this tree was felled, twenty-four other trees simultaneously grew up in that place; each of those trees, with their branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits, became increasingly lush and abundant.
Furthermore, upon each tree there was a golden-beaked bird sporting; its body was adorned with various colors and its voice was pure and exquisite.
When the king saw this, his anger flared up even more, and he sought out an axe for himself, intending to cut down one of the trees.
Wherever the axe reached, ambrosia flowed forth.
Upon seeing this, the king immediately conceived faith and regret, and issued an order to summon the man who had previously planted the tree.
At that time, the man, who had been bound and fettered, was now released and hurried to the king’s presence.
The King asked again:
"For what reason did you plant but a single tree, which immediately produced sprouts, stems, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit?
After I had it cut down, twelve trees grew up, adorned with the seven treasures, vast and beyond compare."
In this way, though they were cut down, they grew back again, even doubling in size compared to before.
The extraordinary songs of various birds were most rare and marvelous.
Yet when I planted trees, they could not even grow immediately, let alone produce flowers, fruit, or any such adornments.
"What is the meaning of this?
You should speak the truth.
That person replied:
"Great King! It is due to the power of my merit that it has come to pass in this way.
He further said:
"Great King! This is brought about by the power of my merit.
When the ministers heard these words, they were all greatly incensed and thought to themselves:
"How can this man boast of his own power of merit before the King?
They then rebuked him together, saying:
"You foolish man, how can you boast of your merit before the King?"
"If this is so, do you not surpass the king, or are you his equal?
At that time, the man bowed his head in reverence toward the ministers and officials and spoke these verses:
"I do not delight in the royal throne, nor in the vast accumulation of wealth and treasures."
Having long ago made the most supreme vows, you have become a Buddha, the Honored One among two-legged beings.
Although you have reached the realm of nirvana, you do not abide in quiescent extinction;
through the power of skillful means and vows, you appear within the world.
He preaches the Dharma to deliver sentient beings, causing them all to reach the other shore;
freed from bonds and possessing sovereignty, they attain the highest peace and happiness.
Because of my past karma, I am now bound by the king.
"Since the power of my supreme vows is thus, may my karma be completely extinguished.
At that time, there were further twenty-four koṭis of golden-beaked birds flying through the air, producing pure and wondrous sounds and playing various musical instruments.

At that time, thirty-two thousand exquisite jewel pavilions simultaneously appeared; each pavilion was twenty-five *yojanas* in height and breadth. Between those pavilions, twenty-five *koṭis* of golden-beaked birds gathered upon each one, reciting this verse:
“Great King, for what reason have you given rise to an evil mind?”
When he cut down that lovely tree that had just sprouted, by the Buddha’s supernatural power, within a single kṣaṇa, it grew back twice, six times, and even ten times its size.
The king, thinking "I too shall plant a tree," planted one; yet it produced no sprouts, stems, flowers, or fruit.
Seeing such a thing, faith did not arise in him; instead, his afflictions increased and he gave rise to anger.
"Because of the King's power of goodness, faith will later arise; in the future, he shall certainly obtain the most supreme fruit.
At that time, the King said, "The voice from the sky is most virtuous and excellent."
"With what intention did I originally conceive the thought of causing destruction? Now that I have attained faith, I deeply repent and reproach myself.
At that time, the King again heard a voice from the air saying:
"Great King!..."
"The one who planted that tree first shall attain Buddhahood and appear in the world as the Honored One of devas and humans.
The king then looked up and asked the worthy one in the air,
"For what reason did the person who planted the next tree fail for the tree to grow?"
The voice from the sky replied:
"Great King, you should know that this person has extensively created sinful karma and possesses not even a slight root of virtue; for these reasons, everything has been destroyed."

At that time, because the roots of goodness of that king had long been matured, upon seeing such a rare event and hearing these words from the air, he gave rise to a superior and most excellent mind of goodness; at that moment, he immediately attained abiding in the equal and wholesome dharmas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
“Those thirty koṭis of ministers, through the power of their matured roots of goodness, likewise abide in those ten stages of the Dharma.

At that time, having heard these words spoken by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja produced great joy and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence. With palms joined in reverence, he stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"For what reason did those kings of old immediately attain stable abiding in the dharmas of those ten stages?
The Buddha said to Bhaiṣajyarāja:
"Those kings and their ministers have long ago received the prediction from the Tathāgatas that they shall all attain Buddhahood."

Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that those trees which were planted were all manifested through the supernatural power of the Buddhas; today I have again manifested this very same thing, no different from what occurred in the past.

At that time, from the gateway of his face, the World-Honored One emitted eighty-four thousand rare, pure, and wondrous rays of light amidst the assembled multitude. Each of these individual rays possessed countless hundreds of thousands of colors, namely:

blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, purple, azure, and green. Having universally illuminated boundless worlds with such various colored rays, the light returned, circled the Buddha’s body to the right, and re-entered through the crown of the World-Honored One’s head.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja joined his palms in reverent salutation, prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, and addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
by what causes and conditions have you emitted this rare and vast radiance that universally illumines the world?”
“If there were no causes and conditions, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha would not emit this light.
I pray that the Buddha, out of his great compassion, will briefly explain it for us.
The Buddha said to Bhaiṣajyasena:
"Do you now see those who come from every direction— the countless multitudes of people from all worlds who have all gathered here at this great assembly?
Bhaiṣajyasena replied, "No."
“World-Honored One!
I do not see it now.
The Buddha said:
“You should examine this with careful scrutiny and observe it repeatedly.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, receiving the Buddha’s holy command, surveyed all four directions as well as above and below. Then, in the eastern quarter, he saw a great tree, exquisitely adorned and magnificent, measuring seven thousand *yojanas* in height and breadth. Twenty-five *koṭis* of people surrounded it on all sides as they entered the Buddha’s assembly; before the World-Honored One, they offered no salutation nor spoke a word, remaining silent and still as they stood to one side of the Buddha.
The same was true for the south, west, north, above, and below.
At that time, having witnessed these events, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyasena came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“I have a slight doubt and wish to pose a question; I pray that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, will explain it for me in detail.
The Buddha said to Bhaiṣajyasena, “Since you now have a doubt, ask whatever you wish; I shall explain each point to you one by one.”
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Now, in each of these great trees throughout the worlds of the four directions, above, and below, there are multitudes of people who have surrounded them on all sides and entered this assembly; they remain silent, without speaking, each staying to one side.”
"For what cause and condition is the matter thus?
The Buddha said to Bhaiṣajyarāja:

"If you now wish to know the causes and conditions of that matter, you may go yourself to that world in that direction and personally ask each of those Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; they will surely explain it to you according to reality."
The Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
Having received your instructions, I shall now go in person to the world-systems in various directions to inquire of those World-Honored Ones.”
"But by what spiritual power can I go there?
The Buddha said,
"You should go to those worlds by your own spiritual power, and I shall further empower you with my own spiritual power."
The Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja then circumambulated the Buddha three times within the assembly and vanished from sight.

From there, he traveled eastward through ninety-six koṭis of worlds until he reached a world named Candrapradīpa. There resided a Buddha named Candrottara-viṣaya, who was endowed with the ten titles, and who was teaching the Dharma surrounded by an assembly of eighty koṭis of great bodhisattvas.
Once the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja had arrived there, he immediately prostrated with his head at the feet of that Buddha, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed that Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

In the presence of Śākyamuni Buddha in this Sahā world, I saw to the east a great tree, exquisitely adorned and magnificent, measuring seven thousand *yojanas* in height and breadth. Twenty-five thousand *koṭis* of people surrounded it on all sides as they entered the Buddha’s assembly; the same was likewise true for the south, west, north, the zenith, and the nadir.
I do not know the causes and conditions for this matter; Śākyamuni Buddha, the Lord of Transformations, has sent me here. I ask you myself for the reason.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will resolve my doubts.
At that time, the Tathāgata Candrāvadāta-viṣaya addressed the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja-sena, saying: "Noble son!

The great trees that have come to that Buddha’s assembly are vast and most excellent, capable of performing the work of a Buddha in that direction. Those multitudes of people are born from those trees in order to manifest the supernatural powers of the Buddhas."
The Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja again addressed that Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This matter is rare; I have never heard of it before, much less been able to see it.”
Furthermore, World-Honored One!

Now, within this assembly, countless multitudes stand before the World-Honored One, surrounding him on all sides so that there is no space between them; these people can barely accommodate their own bodies, yet none of them can see those two arms.
"What is the meaning of this?
We pray that the Buddha will explain it for us. That Buddha said:
“Good son! Whether these multitudes of people are walking or standing, or whether they are bending or stretching, they all encounter no obstruction.
Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja then addressed that Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
There is something I do not yet understand.
What is the meaning of this?”
That Buddha said,
"Good son! Would you now like to see these multitudes of people extend their arms?"
The Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja said, “I now desire to see it; I pray that the Buddha will reveal it.
At that time, the Tathāgata Candrāvabhāsa-viṣaya extended his golden arm within the assembly and displayed it universally to the great multitude.
At that time, the assembly of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of people simultaneously extended one arm each, and from every single one there fell countless hundreds of thousands of kinds of incense—
namely, unguents, powdered incense, and so forth— as an offering to the Buddha.
At that time, that Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja-sena, saying: "Good son,
do you now see this multitude of people, each extending a single arm, raining down various wonderful incenses as an offering to the World-Honored One?"
He replied, "I have seen them. That Buddha said:
“Good son! You should now know that these hundreds of thousands of koṭis of people have all been born through transformation, like what is seen in a dream.
At that time, having witnessed this event, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyasena addressed that Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If these multitudes of people, in a mere instant, each extend but one arm, they are still able to rain down those countless sublime fragrances; how much more so if they were all made to extend both arms, raining down such fragrances and the like in even greater abundance?”
That Buddha said: "So it is, so it is!

Son of good family, all such beings as these are transformations produced by the supernatural power of the Tathāgata, and they are immeasurable. The realms of sentient beings are likewise: whether arising or ceasing, they are like dreams and like illusions; all conditioned phenomena are devoid of any real dharma."
The Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja further addressed that Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Among the various classes of sentient beings, are there those who have been born for a short time and those who have been born for a long time?"
That Buddha said, "So it is. Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja said:
"What is it that is called 'newly born,' and what is it that is called 'long-lived'?
That Buddha replied:
"Among the hundreds of thousands of koṭis of people currently in this assembly, those who have just extended a single arm to rain down incense are those who have been born for a long time;
those born from trees at the place of Śākyamuni Buddha in that Sahā world are those who have been newly born."
The Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja further addressed that Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I now wish to see again that one who was first born; I pray that the Buddha will reveal him.”
At that time, the Tathāgata Candrāvabhāsa-viṣaya immediately extended his right arm once more.

Thereupon, hundreds of thousands of koṭis of people from the four directions, as well as twenty-five koṭis each from the zenith and the nadir, simultaneously entered the Buddha’s assembly. They likewise did not offer greetings to the Buddha, nor did they speak anything; remaining silent and voiceless, they stood to one side of the Buddha.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja addressed the Buddha,
saying: "World-Honored One,
how is it that these countless multitudes of people have entered this Buddha-assembly in a single kṣaṇa, and each remains silent, standing to one side of the Buddha?"
That Buddha said: "Good son!
These multitudes of people are those newly born; they do not know the dharma of birth, nor do they know the dharma of extinction."
Furthermore, they do not know such phenomena as old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, separation from the beloved, or association with the hated;

nor do they know that suffering and the sensation of suffering do not arise from suffering, and that among all phenomena these are neither to be cultivated nor to be fully understood. How, then, could they now have anything to say?
"Therefore, each remains in stillness.
The Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja further addressed that Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
As the Buddha has said, these multitudes of people are newly born; they do not know from where they have come, nor can they understand any phenomena.
That Buddha said, “Good son!
These sentient beings are not born of karmic retribution, nor are they something that can be produced by any craft or skill.”
It is not produced through the conditions of parents, nor does it arise from association with various sensations;

it is not produced by the causal conditions of past karma, nor does it involve the mental recollection of perceptions such as suffering or sensation. Having arisen, it has no abiding; because it comes from such [a source], there is nothing to be spoken of. Thus, one cannot fully comprehend all phenomena, nor does one give rise to the notions of "I" or "mine."
The Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja further addressed that Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
since this one is named ‘the Newly Born,’ from what has he been born?”
"Furthermore, from what does it cease? That Buddha said, "Good son!"
Just as the Buddha was born, so was he born;
just as the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, so did he enter parinirvāṇa.
O son of good family!
It is like a person who, having violated the king’s law, is bound and imprisoned by the king, remaining for a long time in a dungeon.
Within that prison, it is extremely dark and gloomy, such that it cannot be illuminated by the light of the sun; there, one undergoes great suffering and poison, giving rise to much fear and terror.
At that moment, the prison was suddenly consumed by fire; flames blazed on all four sides, and everyone cried out in alarm, yet those who were imprisoned were still unable to escape.
Upon hearing this, the king immediately dispatched strongmen and employed various skillful means to rescue these people.
Once they were freed from the peril of the hellish fires, they came before the king.
The king said: "I pardon you!
From this day forward, do not commit such criminal offenses again; if you do so again, you shall be bound by them with no prospect of release!"
“Good son! The Tathāgata is also like this:

having already severed all afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion, and having perfected all supramundane wholesome dharmas, he is further able to pacify and eliminate all suffering of illness. Moreover, through various skillful means of great compassion, he rescues and delivers all sentient beings suffering within the six realms of existence, causing each and every one to be freed from their fetters. Just as that sunlight destroys all darkness, it extinguishes all sinful defilements and gives rise to wholesome mental orientations.”
"Good son! Whether born long ago or newly born, may all sentient beings be brought to liberation.
At that time, while that Buddha was preaching this Dharma, a voice from the sky spoke these verses:
“The Tathāgata of Great Compassion, dwelling within a pure land, is born from the seeds of wholesome dharmas; thus cause and effect are never lost.
The Buddha’s realm is pure, and he opens the subtle and wondrous Dharma gates.”
Through the skillful means of great compassion, they deliver all classes of sentient beings.
Guiding them step by step, they cause them all to reach nirvana—
the world of eternal tranquility— wherein all actions are free from defilement.
Since beginningless kalpas, whether long-lived or newly born,
within the three realms and six paths, countless multitudes of sentient beings have gathered.
By the power of the Buddha’s compassionate vows, they all return to the gate of liberation.
"Whether worldly or supramundane, may all universally obtain great benefit and happiness.

At that time, the Tathāgata Candrāvadāna-viṣaya emitted a rare, pure, and wondrous light within the assembly. From within that light, a vast sound emerged, shaking throughout the ten directions, and from within that sound, these words were uttered: "Excellent!
The supernatural power of all Buddhas;
how excellent!
The power of the merit of the sublime Dharma.
Excellent! This great harmonious assembly possesses various inconceivable spiritual transformations. Excellent!
"Proclaiming the sublime Dharma-gate, all sentient beings shall obtain benefit and happiness.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja saw a great radiance and heard such voices in the air extolling and praising [the Buddha]. With palms joined in reverence, he prostrated at the feet of that Buddha and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"For what cause and condition has this radiance been emitted?
That Buddha replied, "Good son!"
"Do you now see those who have newly been born within this assembly?
He replied, "I have seen them."
That Buddha said, "Good son!
These multitudes of people have their faculties and conditions fully matured; on this very day, having heard me preach the Dharma, each and every one shall fulfill the ten stages."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja rose from his seat and leaped into the air to a height of eighty thousand yojanas.
At that moment, there were also eighty thousand koṭis of devas and humans who, from within the sky, rained down various exquisite flowers as an offering to that Buddha.
At that time, those who had been born there each paid homage to the World-Honored One with their heads bowed in reverence.
At that moment, bodhisattvas from the ten directions, as well as all the nāgas, devas, yakṣas, and others, also gathered like clouds.
Then, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja joined his palms in the midst of the sky and, with single-minded devotion, addressed that Buddha in these verses:
“Excellent is the Buddha’s spiritual power, Emitting light and sounding forth a great voice;
Throughout the three thousandfold world system, There is none who does not hear it.”
The sentient beings suffering in the thirty-two hells,
upon hearing this sound, find all their afflictions and distress stilled.
The various hosts of devas throughout the three realms likewise hear this sound.
Each gave rise to a heart of reverence, Rejoicing and offering praise.
Throughout the trichiliocosm, The vast sound was heard everywhere;
by the Buddha’s great supernormal powers, All things shook in six ways.
Thirty thousand koṭis of nāga kings from the great oceans,
having heard this great sound, all came to the Buddha’s assembly.
Thirty thousand koṭis of rākṣasa kings [likewise came].
Hearing this great sound, all came to the Buddha’s assembly;
numbering twenty-five thousand koṭis and niyutas,
hearing this great sound, they all came to the Buddha’s assembly.
Within the palace of Vaiśravaṇa, countless yakṣas,
hearing this great sound, all came to the Buddha’s assembly.
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there were hundreds of thousands of koṭis [of beings].
