By means of their supernormal powers, the bodhisattvas have all come to the Buddha’s assembly.
The Buddha Candrottara-viṣaya, wishing to preach the sublime Dharma-door for sentient beings who have newly been born, has therefore gathered them all like clouds.
At that time, after the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja had spoken these verses, he descended from the air, stood before the Buddha, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed that Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Now all the bodhisattvas who have come to this assembly, as well as all the dragon kings, spirits, and deities, have already gathered; each of them desires to hear the Buddha preach the Dharma.
"Now is precisely the right time; we pray that the Buddha will explain it for us.
That Buddha said, "Good son!

"You should now know that these newly born beings have already distanced themselves from all sinful karma; they are fully endowed with the holy life (*brahmacarya*) and have attained great dharanis. All wholesome dharmas are already perfected for them, and I shall now expound for them the great mass of Dharma."
Then, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja addressed that Buddha once more, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This great assembly thirsts with longing to hear it; we pray that the Buddha will explain it for them.”
The Sūtra of the True Dharma of the Great Assembly Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Four.
The Sūtra of the True Dharma of the Great Assembly Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Five.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Imperial Meritorious Official, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial.
Translated by the Dharma-transmitting Master, the Subject Shi Hu, by Imperial Decree.
At that time, the Tathāgata Candrabhadravimalaviśuddhayaśas addressed the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja-sena, saying:

"You should know that all sentient beings who possess a body experience suffering. Birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, affliction, lamentation, pain, meeting with the hated, separation from the loved, and the failure to obtain what one desires—all such phenomena are entirely suffering. They oppress sentient beings, and they cannot attain liberation."
"All this suffering is most terrifying, yet sentient beings do not hear or understand the meaning of this suffering.

At that time, those who had been newly born within the assembly, upon hearing the Buddha speak these names of the various dharmas of suffering, immediately joined their palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
“We wish to hear the meaning of these various sufferings; we pray that the Buddha will explain them for us.
The Buddha said, “O sons of good family!
"It is not only you who delight in hearing this; all sentient beings are likewise so.
Those who had been born there for the first time again addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One!"
"What is the meaning of what you call 'death'?
The Buddha said,
"O sons of good family!..."
That is to say:
when consciousness ceases and the body disintegrates, it is called death.
When the life of any sentient being is about to end, three kinds of winds arise to bring about its destruction; they are as follows:
The wind that extinguishes consciousness, the wind that moves and transforms consciousness, and the wind that gives rise to consciousness—
these three kinds of winds, when a sentient being’s life is about to end, cause consciousness to disperse and perish, move and transform, and undergo change.
The newly born beings said:
“World-Honored One!
How can that wind which extinguishes consciousness cause the consciousness of sentient beings to cease and their bodies to perish?”
The Buddha said:
"That wind which extinguishes consciousness is further of three kinds, namely:
the sword, the needle, and great force."
"By these three kinds [of causes], one's consciousness is extinguished.
Once consciousness has been extinguished, the body is immediately destroyed.
Thus spoke those who had recently been reborn.
“World-Honored One!
What is meant by ‘name-body’ (nāmakāya)?
The Buddha said:

"The body is what is called like an illusion, like a mirage, and like a heavy burden; it is further like saliva, mucus, putrefied matter, and so forth. Those lacking wisdom fail to realize that birth is a great suffering; yet through the arising of birth, the aggregation of causal conditions, and the continuity of the life-faculty, there is this which lacks reality and is associated with the unlovely—such phenomena are conventionally designated as 'body.'"
The newly born ones said,
"World-Honored One!
What is meant by 'life'?"
"Furthermore, what is called 'extinction'?
The Buddha said:

"That which consciousness sustains and maintains is called life. When the retribution of karma declines and exhausts itself, the phenomena of consciousness disperse; the life-faculty is severed and the physical body is destroyed. Therefore, it is called extinction."
"O sons of good family!

I shall now further explain for you the components of the body. You should know that the human body consists of one *koṭi* of sinews and vessels, eighty-four thousand pores, twelve hundred major and minor joints, and three hundred and eight bones; these together constitute the human body.

Furthermore, there are eighty-four thousand species of worms that share this same human body as their support; within the human body they consume [the flesh] day and night, and these various worms also prey upon one another, whereby all manner of sufferings arise."

Among these eighty-four thousand species of worms, there are two particularly large ones that fight one another for seven days and nights; on the seventh day, one worm dies, and yet another worm continues to fight with it.

When one worm dies, another worm is born again; thus it continues in succession until the time when the person's life is severed, at which point all these classes of worms are completely destroyed and have no further basis for existence.

Ordinary worldlings are unable to awaken to the continuous arising and ceasing of internal and external phenomena characterized by suffering; they do not fear the laws of old age, sickness, and death. Whether encountering favorable or adverse conditions, they engage in mutual conflict, like two worms within a body where suffering arises accordingly, yet they fail to realize that when the body perishes and life ends, nothing at all remains.
"Good sons! Suppose there is an ordinary person whose life is about to end.
A spiritual friend comes to comfort him and asks that person:
"During your present life, have you ever known or seen the various hardships of birth, old age, sickness,
and death? That person replied,
"I have indeed known and seen them."
The spiritual friend said:
"Since you now personally recognize and see such sufferings as these, why do you not give rise to a sense of revulsion and develop a superior resolve?

By planting even a small root of goodness in both worlds, severing all unwholesome dharmas, and practicing all correct conduct—if you can do so, after casting off this retribution, you will be born in a superior realm, free from all fears, and take those wholesome dharmas as your refuge."
Moreover, all the various phenomena of suffering in the world can be clearly distinguished and fully observed.
Have you not heard that when the great earth is struck, it produces a great sound;
and when wholesome dharmas are practiced, they possess great and superior power?

Therefore, planting various wholesome dharmas within the pure lands of the Tathāgatas—namely, by making offerings of flower garlands, ointments, food and drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine to the Tathāgatas and the fourfold assembly of pure disciples consisting of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—such offerings constitute planting the seeds of all wholesome qualities within the Buddha-fields, which shall be able to produce all fruits of goodness.
"Now that you have encountered the appearance of the Great Dharma King in this world, if you do not plant various roots of goodness, it will be of no benefit to you.
Then, the spiritual friend spoke these verses for that ordinary person:
"The Tathāgata has appeared in the world, Beating the great drum of the Dharma;”
He opens the subtle and wondrous Dharma-gate, Causing all beings to enter it.
Universally delivering all sentient beings, He leads them to the quiescent extinction of Nirvāṇa.
Now that you behold these deeds, Why do you not arouse diligence?
At that time, that person also spoke in verse, answering the spiritual friend:
"If one is foolish and lacks wisdom, And further encounters evil friends,
One extensively creates the causes for defiled phenomena, Namely, matters such as lustful desire."
The view of self arises with great intensity; they cause schisms in the Saṃgha, destroy stūpas and monasteries, and lack deep faith in the Triple Gem.
They perform only various evil deeds and do not cultivate the causes and conditions for virtue.
At all times, they constantly give rise to various faults;
they trouble and disturb their parents and fail to develop a heart of reverence and filial piety.
They utter unrighteous speech and lightly slander those who are virtuous and good.
Because of creating these evil causes, one will inevitably fall into hell,
where one’s own body undergoes suffering and affliction, with no one able to provide rescue or protection.
There are the fearsome Saṃghāta, the Pratāpana, and the Avīci hells.
Thus, within these various hells, they undergo all manner of sufferings in succession.
Emerging from these great hells, they enter again into smaller hells— namely,
those of the sword-weapon and the lotus— where their suffering continues without end.
In such great and small hells, there are countless sentient beings who,
according to the causes and conditions of their own karma, receive retribution according to its lightness or gravity;
for a hundred kalpas or a thousand kalpas, or even for a further length of time.
Bound by the ropes of evil karma, there is no way to attain liberation.
That Hell of Weapons is a hundred yojanas in length and breadth;
its gates are not seen, for there are only those who undergo suffering.
Countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of sword-trees and mountain-blades of knives drive those sinners to climb them, their bodies all severed and destroyed.
Though they die and perish for a moment, they are once again blown back by the winds of karma.
Immediately they are reborn again, And undergo all manner of suffering and affliction.
The hells have no bounds, And sentient beings are likewise inexhaustible;
By the causal conditions of their evil karma, They continue in succession without interruption.
I have committed various evil deeds And shall certainly fall into those realms;
O virtuous friend, at this time, Please hear the karma I have created.
Once, driven by a greedy mind, I extensively constructed houses and dwellings.
Adorned with colorful paintings and intricate carvings, and embellished with gold and jewels; furthermore,
he established various gardens and groves, granaries, treasuries, and enterprises,
along with livestock such as oxen and horses— all provided as necessary resources.
The parents and their retinue, both internal and external, were exceedingly numerous;
the servants and female entertainers were likewise beyond measure.
Day and night, they were constantly made to produce various musical sounds through song.
They indulge only in their own pleasure, taking no thought for the suffering of others;
relying on their great wealth and nobility, they create all manner of adornments,
and all the objects they enjoy are made entirely of gold, silver, and precious gems.
Having bathed with scented water, one further anoints the body with various exquisite fragrances, such as camphor, sandalwood, and musk.
Once bathed with scented water, one adorns the body in successive order.
Bracelets and rings were all fashioned from precious gems;
pearl necklaces served as ornaments for the neck, while the finest,
most excellent gold was used for earrings and other such adornments.
Having adorned his body, he wears upon his head various exquisite flowers— somaṇas, campaka, and other fragrant blossoms.
He further dons magnificent garments, namely the finest fine cotton cloth.
Fresh white and pure, all are perfumed with exquisite fragrances;
the food and drink are of the most supreme flavor, sweet and deliciously aromatic.
Attendants provide whatever is required, so that for a moment there is no thought of hunger or thirst.
Spreading fine rugs upon the ground, one walks and travels about;
with attendants on both sides, one is autonomous and noble.
Thus, adorned extensively in this manner, one takes delight in that body.
Constantly cherishing and guarding it, one does not conceive thoughts of destruction.
Once possessed of abundant wealth and pleasure, with nothing further to desire,
one indulges the mind of defiled passion and commits unwholesome transgressions.
The eye craves for the realm of forms, and so it is with all the sense faculties;
they are the cause of faults, yet one cannot perceive this oneself.
In the spheres of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, the various afflictions arise accordingly.
Within objects that are favorable or adverse, the phenomena of greed, hatred, and delusion arise.
Through various contacts such as softness and so forth, contact with body and mind gives rise to craving;
once that perception of craving has arisen, all sinful karmas are committed.
Once, in a moment of heedlessness, I harmlessly harmed a sentient being;
with an arrow I struck a deer’s body, causing its life to be extinguished.
I took only its meat, without giving thought to the world beyond.
One must experience the retribution for oneself; who can take its place?
I was foolish and lacked wisdom, caring only for the nourishment of my body.
When the suffering of death arrives one day, consciousness ceases and the body perishes.
There is only the accumulation of all suffering and affliction; not a single heart finds it lovable.
Parents and all kinsmen look upon one another but cannot save.
Even skilled physicians and wondrous medicines exert their efforts in vain.
It only increases the heart’s sorrow and distress, with no means of rescue or relief.
Once my life has come to an end and I am cast away in the Śītavana charnel ground,
I shall become food for birds, beasts, and various insects, who will devour me until I am fully satiated.
All things are non-existent; illusory phenomena appear before us.
All objective realms are entirely empty, yet karmic retribution alone is never lost.
At such a time, there is nothing to rely upon; only wholesome dharmas can be taken as a refuge.
Just as I have created the causes of evil, I shall surely fall into hell.
Having extensively accumulated a mass of karmic offenses, suffering and affliction will subsequently arise;
throughout those three periods of time, I shall destroy the seeds of wholesome dharmas.
The two dharmas of sensation and mental formations have contact as their cause;
because of contact, various cravings arise, resulting in the bonds of sorrow and suffering.
Wholesome dharmas are like excellent medicine, capable of curing the craving mind.
Since greed and the like do not arise, one cannot commit any evils.
Truly, I lack merit and wisdom, having received this human body in vain;
yet the Buddha has proclaimed the gates of skillful means, such as giving and upholding the precepts.
I cannot act for myself; I do not rejoice in what is seen or heard, nor can I listen to the True Dharma. Thus, ignorance increases day by day.
Afflictions such as nescience revolve along with it without end.
Obstructed by the causes and conditions that hinder wholesome dharmas, by what means can one attain liberation?
With a deluded and distracted mind, there is not even a moment of peaceful abiding;
scorched by the fires of affliction, one undergoes various forms of bondage.
Within the body there is not the slightest pleasure; delight in the Dharma does not arise even for a moment.
Life will not last long; all things are subject to destruction.
Only the supreme Dharma of the Buddhas can rescue sentient beings from suffering.
The Dharma-gate of the True Precepts: those who ascend it attain great bliss.
Just as I have committed karmic deeds, I feel deep remorse within myself;
now having encountered a virtuous friend, I therefore speak according to reality.
At that time, the Tathāgata Candrāvadānacaryā addressed the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, saying:
"Good son! When ordinary beings approach the end of their lives, they give rise to great terror and distress in their hearts, finding no one to provide them with protection."
"Only various wholesome dharmas can serve as a basis for a sublime karmic fruition, such that nothing is lost.
At that time, that Buddha spoke these verses:
"When sentient beings commit evil deeds, They will certainly fall into hell."
In hunger they swallow iron balls; in thirst they drink molten copper.
From their bodies fierce flames burst forth, burning themselves through the power of their evil karma.
Their limbs and members are all shattered as they undergo great suffering of terror.
They do not see pleasant objects, nor do they hear the name of the True Dharma;
oppressed only by suffering in body and mind, everything is unlovely to them.
When sentient beings perform wholesome deeds, they will certainly be reborn in the happy realms.
Encountering virtuous friends, they are exhorted to cultivate wholesome dharmas.
Giving rise to right faith and understanding, possessing precepts, wisdom, and much learning,
all afflictions are extinguished, and they attain perfect enlightenment.
Vigorous practice is supreme; it is that which the Buddhas who appear in the world have proclaimed.
It rouses all roots of goodness and gives rise to no retreat or despondency.
Compassion is the true brahmacarya; it gathers in all sentient beings.
Benefiting oneself and further benefiting others, Causing all to attain liberation.
Son of good family, listen attentively!
That which the Buddha speaks is the truth; he utters the subtle and wondrous sound of Dharma, Causing all beings to be tamed.
Great compassion is the father, the bodhicitta is the mother;
with wholesome dharmas as spiritual friends, one is able to rescue and protect sentient beings.
When the Perfectly Awakened One appears in the world, he proclaims the most supreme Dharma-gate.
Through skillful means, he transforms sentient beings, Causing them to dwell in the ground of quiescent extinction.
The Buddha is the one of great compassion, The most supreme Honored One in the world;
Universally observing all sentient beings, He regards them all equally as his own children.
"Equally and without duality, may all beings take refuge.
At that time, when that Buddha preached this Dharma, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja joined his palms in reverent salutation and addressed that Buddha, saying:
"By what causes and conditions does this great earthquake occur?
I pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will explain this to me."
That Buddha said:
"Good son! You should observe the four directions; what do you see?"

At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, receiving the Buddha’s holy command, immediately surveyed the four directions and saw this great earth trembling; in a short moment it split open, and sixty-five koṭis of people emerged from the earth.
At that time, the sixty-five koṭis of those who had been born first all joined their palms and addressed the Buddha together, saying:
"From what source have we been born?
Within the assembly, the Buddha pointed to the aforementioned ones who had been born first and said to those born from the earth:
“O sons of good family!
Do you see this multitude of people? They replied:
“I have seen it,” they replied. The Buddha said,
“Just as they were born, so too are you.”
The one born from the earth further asked:
"Should these multitudes of people be extinguished?
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is! They have all ceased.
O sons of good family!"
"It is not only this assembly; all sentient beings shall likewise return to extinction.
At that time, those who had first been born into the Buddha's assembly each rose with palms joined and addressed that Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"As the Buddha has taught, we detest and find no delight in the two phenomena of birth and death.
The Buddha said,
"Since you are already able to detest birth and death, why are you unable to arouse diligence?"
Then those newly born beings addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We have heard and received the True Dharma in the presence of the Tathāgata. We see that this assembly of Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas is endowed with great supernormal powers and majestic virtue; this is what we delight in. We, too, desire to advance toward its cultivation and practice, so as to remain far removed from birth and death.”

At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja saw others who had arisen from the earth. Immediately, together with five hundred great bodhisattvas, each by means of their own supernormal power, they leaped into the air from within that assembly to a height of twenty thousand yojanas. In mid-air, they manifested various postures: some displayed the manner of walking, some the posture of sitting cross-legged, some the stride of a lion king, some the stride of an elephant king, and some the strides of various exotic beasts. Having manifested these various forms, they further performed diverse miraculous transformations in the sky.
At that time, each of these bodhisattvas possessed a bodily radiance in the void that was like the light of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of suns and moons.
Then, all those who had been born from the earth addressed that Buddha together, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"For what cause and condition does this vast radiance exist,
and why do these various miraculous and rare phenomena manifest in the sky?
The Buddha said:
“O sons of good family!
Do you see these bodhisattvas dwelling in mid-air? They replied:
“I have seen them,” he replied.

The Buddha said, “This great radiance is the individual body-light of these bodhisattvas; each and every one of these bodhisattvas is capable of manifesting various supernormal powers, transformations, and such deeds.”
At that time, the assembly of bodhisattvas, including Bhaiṣajyarāja and others, immediately produced a subtle and wondrous sound from mid-air and addressed the Buddha together, saying:

“We pray that the Buddha, out of his great compassion, will proclaim the essential Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings; if gods or humans should hear this Dharma, they shall all attain the most supreme benefit and peace.”

At this time, we have all been established through the power of the Tathāgata’s great compassion, skillful means, diligence, and vows; we pray that the Buddha will now manifest the light of the Dharma to universally illuminate the world.
Having spoken these words, they both descended from the sky and stood before the Buddha.
That Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja: "Noble son!"
"Do you now see this trichiliocosm shaking in six ways?
The Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja said,
"I have seen it."
World-Honored One!
Nevertheless, we are currently unable to understand for what reason such a thing has occurred.
Furthermore, I now have a slight doubt and wish to ask the World-Honored One; may you please resolve it for us.
That Buddha said, "Good son! You now have doubts;
ask whatever you wish. Whether concerning matters of the past, future, or present—of the three periods of time—I shall explain each one to you in accordance with reality."
The Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja addressed that Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

For what reason are there in this assembly eighty-four thousand multitudes of devaputras, eighty-four koṭis of great bodhisattvas, twelve thousand koṭis of nāga kings, eighteen thousand koṭis of bhūtas, and twenty-five thousand koṭis of piśācas? By what meaning is it that the number of such multitudes is so vast?”
That Buddha said: "Good son!

You should know now that all these great assemblies have gathered together; they have all come here to listen to the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma, and on this very day they shall attain great benefit and joy, forever emerging from saṃsāra."

Furthermore, among them, some attained stable abiding in the ten stages (daśabhūmi); some attained stable abiding in the realm of nirvāṇa; some attained liberation from the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death, dwelling in the dharma of peace and bliss; some attained liberation from the bonds of afflictions (kleśa); and some attained deep entry into the Buddha’s true dharma.
The Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja further addressed that Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The Tathāgata skillfully performs all manner of expedient works for the sake of all sentient beings, guiding and transforming them in accordance with their needs; how could there be any weariness or indolence therein?”
That Buddha said:
"Good son, listen attentively!
The Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion and establishes various skillful means to universally gather in all sentient beings, causing them all to attain liberation, never wearying throughout."

However, ordinary beings are deluded regarding wholesome dharmas; although they may encounter a Tathāgata, they are unable to draw near to him, listen to his teachings, receive them, or practice them, nor do they seek liberation.

"Good son! Today, amidst this great assembly, the Tathāgata blows the great Dharma conch, beats the great Dharma drum, utters the great Dharma sound, and expounds the great Dharma meaning. Whether they be devas or nāgas, or even the eight classes of beings and the fourfold assembly, as well as all those who have newly been born—all such members of the great assembly today attain the great dhāraṇī, perfect the wholesome dharmas, abide securely in the ten stages (bhūmis), and universally obtain benefit and joy."

All of these are produced through the skillful means of the Tathāgata’s supernormal powers, causing all sentient beings to abide on the stage of diligence and attain the perfection of the Dharma, just like the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
At that time, from among the sixty-five koṭis, five thousand who had been born first rose from their seats, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We carry this body as a heavy burden and are deeply terrified; by what means may we be liberated?

Furthermore, all sentient beings dwell within saṃsāra without even a moment of peace; their desires obstruct their minds so that they cannot understand, and they abide in the realm of darkness, unable to see clearly. We only pray that the World-Honored One will take us and all sentient beings under his care, bestow fearlessness upon us, and grant us peace and happiness. We entreat the World-Honored One to proclaim the sublime Dharma, so that sentient beings of little wisdom may increase their right understanding, that all suffering beings may attain liberation, and that in every life they are born, they may behold the Buddha and hear the Dharma.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja addressed those who had just been born, speaking these verses:
“You who desire to hear the True Dharma, First you must sustain your lives with food and drink;
Only after giving rise to a fearless and vast mind Will you deeply attain the flavor of the most supreme and wondrous Dharma.”
The one who was born first also spoke a verse, answering the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja:
“O Venerable One of great wisdom, you who have well-tamed and stilled all your faculties,
you possess a vast reputation and are beloved and revered by all.”
Having perfected all wholesome dharmas, there is nothing you do not know;
why then do you say that food and drink sustain life?
According to our understanding, food and drink are the cause of transgression.
Once consumed, within the belly it becomes various kinds of filth;
though it increases physical form and strength, evil dharmas arise accordingly,
and within the three miserable realms and evil destinies, one shall experience great terror.
The sinful karma of all sentient beings arises entirely from food and drink;
all desires and attachments are produced by food and drink.
The ignorant ones of the world give rise to various kinds of greedy thoughts.
They cultivate vast fields and gardens, buildings, houses, and multi-storied pavilions;
various exquisite garments and ornaments, as well as the most supreme adornments,
and the seven kinds of wonderful treasures, such as necklaces of genuine pearls.
Elephants, horses, and carriages, And numerous male and female servants—
though wealth and status may last but a moment, In the end they all return to the law of impermanence.
When one's lifespan is exhausted, One wanders through the various realms of existence.
Unable to hear the True Dharma, one is far removed from virtuous friends.
Even if one were to become a Wheel-Turning King over the four great continents,
possessing all seven treasures and a full retinue of a thousand sons;
Wealthy, noble, and possessing great sovereignty, Valiant and majestic,
they are the refuge of all, To whom everyone pays homage and offers praise.
Yet even these superior rewards of an entire lifetime Are likewise impermanent.
When their lifespan has come to an end, they must experience the fruits of their good and evil karma.
Though they may possess precious jewels, or be courageous and of great majesty,
when their life is exhausted, no personal power can save them.
Venerable One, as I have said, there is nothing whatsoever upon which to rely;
only the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are the true refuge.
Like a father and like a mother, they are able to nourish and bring one forth.
Loving with impartiality, regarding all beings as one's own children;
like the light of the sun and moon, universally illuminating all darkness,
may all the sufferings of saṃsāra be severed and extinguished so that they never arise again.
Uprooting the roots of those afflictions, Causing them to be free from all fears,
May you cause all classes of sentient beings To realize unsurpassed bodhi;
Proclaiming the gateway of the True Dharma, May you cause them to abide in non-retrogression.
Worldly food and drink bring no benefit but only faults;
one cannot be reborn among the gods, nor do they yield desirable fruits.
There is no true happiness in the world, for they will surely summon the retribution of extreme suffering.
Diminishing one's lifespan, one creates the causes for unwholesome karma;
Giving rise to craving for wealth and pleasure, one fails to comprehend impermanence.
Failing to perform the most supreme deeds, one does not understand the sublime Dharma.
Not mindful, they do not leave behind their faults, nor do they abide in a tranquil mind.
Once their lifespan has ended, they undergo various sufferings in the realms of existence;
struck by the staff of impermanence and bound by the ropes of the five desires.
Suffering increases ever more, and one cannot escape the retribution of karma;
illuminated by past deeds, there is no rescue and no refuge.
One should recognize that when the Dharma perishes, it will only increase sorrow, affliction, and fear.
I would rather bestow upon all people precious treasures, gold, silver, and crystal, never giving rise to stinginess;
I would rather use my own physical strength to serve as a servant for others.
Even if it should last for such a long time, I would never grow weary.
If the thought of craving and attachment arises, leading to the vast accumulation of various treasures and the finest delicacies of food and drink, I immediately feel fear.
May the Venerable One listen attentively to what we say:
even if those various devas were to receive the retribution of supreme and wondrous bliss,
with vessels made of exquisite jewels filled with all kinds of superior flavors, [they would still not equal this].
Sweet and fragrant, those who eat it experience delight;
they increase the stature, physical strength, and majestic power of the devas and humans.
Yet when that retribution comes to an end, none of it is real.
For this reason, we do not take delight in food and drink,
but find joy only in the gateway of the True Dharma, seeking liberation from all sufferings.
Having distanced ourselves from the bonds of craving and attachment, we have attained sovereignty and unimpededness.
I take refuge in the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the Great Sage and True Saint.
O Venerable One of Great Wisdom, I pay homage to you with reverence;
endowed with vast compassion, all sentient beings delight in beholding you.
"What is your name? I pray that the Honored One will tell me; if I see, hear, or rejoice in it, my faculties shall attain purity.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja further spoke in verse, answering the newly born one:
“If you now wish to hear my name, know that all those names are known only to the Buddha;
when hundreds of thousands of koṭis of beings are first born, the Buddha alone can discern each and every one of their names.”
That newly born one then spoke a verse, saying:
"I have personally heard from the Buddha that among all names—whether for those newly born or long-born—yours alone is the most profound; I have never heard the Buddha explain it at such length."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja further spoke in verse, answering the newborn one:
"Know my name; I am called Bhaiṣajyarāja. Because I save sentient beings with wondrous medicines, I have obtained this title."
All classes of sentient beings are entangled by various ailments;
through the gateway of skillful means, I provide relief in accordance with their needs.
Greed is the greatest ailment, causing affliction and harm throughout the world.
With this disease as their cause, all manner of faults arise.
The disease of anger is like a great fire that incinerates the mind of tranquility;
only the medicinal elixir of the Dharma can eliminate all such suffering and affliction.
The disease of delusion is most terrifying; it submerges the mind of wisdom.
One dies and falls into the evil realms, unable to hear the True Dharma.
From these three diseases, all other ailments arise in succession.
For those further deluded by the darkness of ignorance, I bestow the medicine of the Dharma upon them all.
May they universally be freed from faults, extinguish all karmic causes,
and bring an end to suffering so that it does not arise again, forever severing all fears.
Having attained freedom from all ailments, may you swiftly behold the Honored One of Perfect Enlightenment;
through me, the King of Wondrous Physicians, medicine is administered according to each ailment.
All classes of sentient beings are constantly being consumed by fire.
Blazing, it cannot be extinguished; it gives rise further to various sufferings and afflictions.
Greed and desire act as a heavy burden, and there is no time of liberation from them.
Hatred and delusion are likewise; they successively increase one’s faults.
Though constantly burdened by heavy loads, they do not seek the gate of liberation;
nor do they contemplate impermanence, nor reflect upon the path of renunciation.
Afflictions and karma pursue them, yet they remain unaware of their suffering.
When various ailments press upon the body, one cannot seek the wondrous medicine.
Due to the cause of ignorance, the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) arise accordingly;
once these factors such as the formative forces have arisen, the fault of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is produced.
All conditioned phenomena are not ultimate; all dharmas are empty.
Without wisdom one cannot know this, and thus there is no way to give rise to right mindfulness.
If one does not cultivate the practice of tranquility, consciousness will cease and suffering will increase.
Throughout incalculable eons, they were unable to attain liberation.
Now that the Buddha has appeared in the world as the Teacher of gods and humans,
he reveals the path of perfect enlightenment, just as parents cherish their children.
Furthermore, he rains down the great treasure of the Dharma, universally saving all sentient beings;
yet those with deviant wisdom who do not embrace the True Dharma are excluded.
Those who have resolved to attain Bodhicitta shall enter the gateway of the True Dharma.
Realizing that all conditioned phenomena are empty, one is unimpeded even within emptiness.
If one realizes that emptiness is selfless, there is nothing whatsoever upon which to rely;
all afflictions are likewise empty, and one remains far removed from all faults.
At that time, those who had been born first spoke these verses:
“The Bodhisattva of Great Compassion universally rescues all sentient beings;
The Great King of Physicians, through his diligence, remains untiring for a long time.”
"Reflecting upon the suffering of saṃsāra, and sustained by merit,
I take refuge with true faith and arouse courageous diligence.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja further spoke these verses:
"You should now know: the Buddha is the most supreme Honored One;
in both the mundane and supramundane realms, he is fully endowed with merit and wisdom.
He possesses the thirty-two marks and is adorned with the manifold secondary characteristics."
With supreme great compassion, you extensively deliver all classes of beings.
The Buddha’s majestic appearance is lofty and manifest, like Mount Sumeru;
his wisdom is inexhaustible, like that great ocean.
"Skillfully opening all expedient means, he transforms sentient beings according to their needs;
through beholding, paying homage, and taking refuge, all obtain the fruit of peace and happiness.

At that time, the Tathāgata Candrāvabhāsa-viṣaya emitted a voice as pure and wondrous as that of the kalaviṅka bird, heard throughout the ten directions, and from his face issued eighty-four thousand rays of light of various colors, namely:

Blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, purple, azure, and green—such light, vast and blazing, universally illumined the trichiliocosm; all the thirty-two great hells were utterly destroyed by the light’s radiance, and wherever the light shone upon the celestial palaces, they were filled with expansive brilliance.
After this radiance had illuminated the trichiliocosm, further, from within that light, all the articles of enjoyment belonging to all sentient beings emerged and appeared in the void.
Having performed such a transformation, the light circled back around the Buddha seven times and then entered through the crown of that Buddha’s head.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja rose from his seat, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed that Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"For what cause and condition does he thus repeatedly emit great rays of light that universally illuminate the world?
At that time, that Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja-senāpati, saying:
“Good son! Today I perform a great Buddha-work; because there are sentient beings in this assembly who have attained great benefit and joy, for this reason I again emit light.”
The Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja again addressed that Buddha, saying:
“I have a doubt that I wish to ask about; I only pray that the World-Honored One will resolve it for me.”
That Buddha said,
"Good son! Regarding what you have doubted, you shall ask as you wish."
The Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja said:
"World-Honored One,
for what reason does the World-Honored One manifest various rare and marvelous phenomena for those newly born into this assembly, and further proclaim this subtle and wondrous Dharma-gate?"
"Regarding those who have lived for a long time, why is it that the World-Honored One does not treat them all in this same way?
Is it that these types of beings are unable to understand the Buddha’s True Dharma? That Buddha said:
“Good son! Why do you now speak such words, posing this question before the Tathāgata?
This cannot be called speech that is compliant and so forth. For what reason?

The Tathāgata transforms and delivers all sentient beings with impartiality, preaching the Dharma in accordance with skillful means; all who hear it obtain benefit, fully attain entry into the gates of all dhāraṇīs, and accomplish all meritorious virtues.
At that time, there further appeared in the sky above the Buddha countless vast and exquisite pavilions made of the seven precious jewels.
Then, that Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja-sena, saying:
"O son of good family!
"Do you now see this exquisite pavilion?
The Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja replied,
"I have seen it."
"World-Honored One! That Buddha said,
"You should now know that all of these are collectively manifested by those who have newly been born."
Why is this? Because on this very day, all those who have newly been born shall fulfill all wholesome dharmas;

furthermore, today I shall beat the great Dharma drum, whereby countless devas and humans will attain the perfection of the Dharma, and countless beings in the hells will be freed from their suffering and affliction.
Furthermore, there were countless sentient beings who, for a brief moment, gave rise to right mindfulness and took refuge in the Buddha’s wisdom; they all attained liberation.

When that Buddha spoke these words, ninety-nine thousand *koṭis* of sentient beings who had been born for a long time in the assembly realized the fruit of *srotāpanna*. They attained perfection in the Dharma, severed their karmic obstructions, and became far removed from all suffering. All such as these were born from the True Dharma of the Tathāgata.

At that time, fifty koṭis of bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, came from the east and entered that assembly; sixty koṭis of bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, came from the south and entered that assembly; seventy koṭis of bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, came from the west and entered that assembly; eighty koṭis of bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, came from the north and entered that assembly; ninety koṭis of bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, came from the nadir and entered that assembly; and one hundred koṭis of bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, came from the zenith and entered that assembly.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja addressed that Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
why is it that the entirety of space has become the two colors of crimson and black?"
That Buddha said:
"Good son! Do you not now know such causes and conditions?"
He replied: "World-Honored One!
I am unable to know."
That Buddha said: "Only a Buddha, a Tathāgata, knows and observes this himself.
O son of good family!"
"You should now know that from the worlds of the various directions, there have come to this Buddha’s assembly bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of many koṭis of Gaṅgā rivers.

Thus, once the hosts of bodhisattvas had arrived from their respective directions, they descended from the sky and stood before the Buddha; they prostrated at the feet of that Buddha and each withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja addressed that Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
by what causes and conditions has this great assembly of bodhisattvas gathered here once again?"
That Buddha said,
"Good son! This great assembly of bodhisattvas has gathered because they all take those who have just been born as their object of focus for generating the aspiration [for enlightenment]."

When that Buddha spoke these words, all those who had recently been born within the assembly immediately attained the full perfection of all dharmas and became securely established in the tenth bhūmi.

Furthermore, within that Buddha’s assembly, there were countless practitioners of the bodhisattva path who all attained stable abiding in the dharmas of bodhisattvas and acquired great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
All sentient beings who saw, heard, or rejoiced in these [teachings] obtained benefit and happiness.
All those who have already established themselves upon the bodhisattva stages shall no longer regress, but will further increase, excel, and solidify their bodhisattva practices and dharmas.

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the great bodhisattvas such as Samantavīra, the great bhikṣus such as Ājñātakauṇḍinya, and the entire assembly—including gods, humans, and asuras of the world—having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced, and they faithfully accepted and practiced it.
The Sūtra on the True Dharma of the Great Assembly Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Five.
